speechtext: ['The evening is still quite early and if my hon. friend desires an adjournment I do not wish to press him to go on.']

Mr. Speaker. On account of the agitation which has been going on throughout the Dominion, particularly during the past year, with reference to the tariff question, I think it is the duty of every member of this House to place himself on record as to what he considers is the best fiscal policy for this country. There are certain deterent influences, Sir, which might prevent a person not much accustomed to public speaking from addressing this House at this time. I mentioned last year, and the same thing applies this year, that one very deterent influence especially for young members, is the lack of attention which is paid to speeches i in this House, and the very few members who remain in the Chamber while the debate Is going on. There is another influence which may perhaps deter some members from speaking much in this House of Commons. It is this. If the mathematical calculation of our friend from West Elgin (Mr. Robinson) is correct, the expense of running this House is $28 a minute, and some of us may be afraid to score up a very large bill against the Dominion, for fear our electors may call us to account for it when we return home. For instance, the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Bell) who closed the debate last evening ran up a bill of $3,380, if the calculation of the hon. member for Elgin is correct. Some of us may have some doubt as to whether the speech was worth it or not, but that is a matter for the hon. member to settle with his constituents.
What about the member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) ?	[DOT]
I have not had sufficient time at my disposal to figure up his account.
He would have a big bill.

This debate lins gone on for several days and some twenty members have spoken. Some of them have done what I intend to do before I sit down, namely, to give my own views regarding the best fiscal policy for this country, but in the case of a great many of them it would be very hard to ascertain just what their views were. I am free to admit that
every member of this House must be to a certain extent influenced, it may be imperceptibly, by the environment in which be is placed. I do not mean by this that I think it is the duty of every member to try and square himself with his constituents, although probably there may be a temptation to do that. It is my idea, but of course I may be wrong, that one of the objects which a great many members of this House must have in speaking at such length as they do, is in order to get their speeches down on ' Hansard ' and circulated through the country and in their constituencies. Apart from that I cannot see very much use in a great many of these speeches which are delivered, probably late in the evening, when there is barely a quorum present, and when those who are present pay little attention to what is being said. What I have said with regard to the environment off members, is based upon the fact that I live in a purely agricultural community. We have not in the county of Huntingdon any manufactures of any importance; not more than would supply the local demands. Our farmers are principally engaged in dairying and pork raising which is a by-product of dairying. Our farmers are to a large extent free traders, or low tariff men at all events. The principle products of the county of Huntingdon are butter and cheese the price of which is fixed by the market in England, and I suppose the same rule would to a large extent apply to our product of pork and hams. The trouble with our people, as with a great many agricultural people is, to know where the compensation comes to them for the increased price they have to pay for manufactured goods by reason of a high tariff. I came to this parliament with my own idea as to what was the best tariff for this country, and that idea was that a low tariff fills the bill. You may call it a revenue tariff or whatever you please, but at all events I am decidedly against any increase in the tariff, and so arc a great many people throughout Canada.
Hear, hear.

My feeling is that we should try to legislate for the masses rather than for the classes. As I have said I came here with my own idea as to the best fiscal policy for the country, and I suppose every member of the House has come here with his mind made up on that question to a greater or lesser extent. But while that is true, I came here also with an open mind ready to be convinced and ready to change my views if the arguments brought forth should lead me to believe that my own ideas were wrong. I must say that so far that I have not changed my mind, but that I have continued to believe that the best policy for this country is a low tariff, or what may be called a revenue tariff. Another thing is that I came

liere a new member; one who probably had not taken that interest In these public matters which he ought to have taken. My principle business in connection with political matters heretofore was simply an anxiety to see that the man of our choice was elected and we generally succeeded in doing that.
Some lion. MEMBERS. Hear, hear.

The word 1 statesman ' is bandied about here, but I must confess that I yet do not know exactly what it means. Some people have a different idea of as to what a statesman is or ought to be, from others, but be that as it may, my opinion is that for a person to make a success in public life it is necessary for him to come here in early life. As the saying is, he ought be caught young. I am afraid that quite a number of members of this House came here when it can hardly be expected that they would be in a position to qualify as statesmen.
I consider, Sir, that the agriculturists of this country have their rights; so does everybody. But, one difficulty in connection with the agriculturists asserting their right is that the manufacturers are organized and they are not. That is no reflection on this government because it would equally apply to all governments, and the fact remains that those people who can bring their views most directly before any government are most likely to get their grievances redressed, or, to get what they want. It is natural to expect that. If you see a particularly well dressed, well groomed, well fed body of men about the Russell House or around the corridors here, and you ask who thev are, in nine cases out of ten you will be told that they are the representatives of the Manufacturers' Association or some kindred organization of that kind, who have come here to place their views before the government, and to try to worry the government into granting their requests. I might say .iust here, that before I came to parliament I never had as much sympathy with the ministers of the Crown as I have had since. I think that they are a much abused lot of men. I think that they have to stand a great deal, and it does make my blood boil when I hear some of the members of the opposition taunting them for the salaries they receive, and for drawing salaries for doing nothing. Why, Sir, I believe that if the ministers were paid according to the annoyance they have to put up with, they would get double their present salaries. Now, Mr. Speaker, the farmers are in an altogether different position from the manufacturers with regard to placing their views before the government. I have not had much to do with manufacturing interests myself, but judging from appearances the manufacturers are pretty well off. The farmers are different. The farmer cannot come to Ottawa to state his case. He has Mr. MACLAREN (Huntingdon).
got to stay at home looking pretty closely after his farm and his stock in order to make ends meet, and there is not much junketing around for him in special cars to come here to interview the government. In that way the manufacturers have a great advantage over the farmers, and seem to get favours which the farmers and the great consuming classes consider are inimical to their best interests. The Manufacturers' Association we have heard so much about appears to be a wonderful combination. Wonderful resolutions they passed at their meeting at Halifax. They were so wonderful that even the Tory ' Gazette ' of Montreal spoke about them adding hypocrisy to folly. These men are organized, and they are in a better position to bring their views before the government than the farmers and the great purchasing classes.
Since I have come to this House, I have heard a great 'many figures and statements quoted to show the condition of the country. I do not take much stock in these things, because it appears to me that the same figures are quoted on both sides to support different arguments. I would rather be guided by my own experience and observation in a matter of this kind. I know that so far as my own county and the adjoining counties are concerned, there is no question about the prosperity of the country. Everybody admits it. Eight or ten years ago the farmers had mortgages on their farms, and were paying 6 or 8 per cent interest on them. These are all wiped out now, the farmers are able to get money at 4 or 4J per cent to pay them off, and the men who a few years ago had to borrow money, have now money to lend. I would rather judge of the prosperity of the country from my knowledge of such facts than from all these statistics.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Bell) who spoke last night, was figuring up what it cost per family and per head to pay the annual revenue received by the government, and he, very pessimistically, I think, came to the conclusion that if the present state of things continued very much longer, the hard times would return, and the people would be in want just as they were when our hon. friends opposite were in power. I know that at present the people have enough to pay their way, and something left over. The deposits in our savings banks and other banks are increasing greatly, which is a sure evidence that the country is prosperous.
What I am going to speak of may be considered ancient history ; but hon. gentlemen in the opposition have been going so far back that I think I have a right to follow suit. Our hon. friends opposite are in a kind of dilemma. When the present tariff was brought in by the hon. Minister of Finance, we all remember the howl that went up from the Conservatives, that it was going to ruin the country. They claimed, as they have always done, to be a highly

protective party. In 1878, when the national policy was introduced, they prophesied that it was going to do many wonderful things which it did not do, and they Intimated that if they got into power again they would reintroduce the national policy, and give the country that prosperity which they failed to give when they were in power. You remember how they promised that industries would spring up all over the country, and that population would flow in and occupy the vacant lands of the North-west, and the farmers would have a fine time raising food to supply the millions who were to work these industrial establishments. We were in fact going to have something approaching the millenium. Such did not turn out to be the case, however. In the census of 1891 there was a great deal of padding in regard to the number of industrial establishments in the country. Some of the padding was done in my own county. Eighteen or twenty squaws who were engaged in making baskets in their cabins were put down as so many industrial establishments. A woman working at a hand-loom in her home, was put down as another industrial establishment. The cobblers working at their benches were enumerated in the same way. But notwithstanding all that padding, the Conservative party failed to show the results which they had promised to bring about under the influence of the beneficent national policy. Now they are obliged to admit that under the tariff policy of this government, the country has not gone to ruin, as they prophesied it would. I will not say they are sorry for that ; I think they are glad that the country is prosperous, though they do not like to admit it. But it is remarkable what a different tone they take now from what they did in 1897, when this tariff was introduced. You remember what a doleful story was told about the ruinous state of things that would ensue under this tariff, and how it was to do away to a certain extent with the beneficent results of the national policy. What is the fact ? Listen to this from a speech by one high in the ranks opposite, our lion, friend opposite :
Now what is the result. The result is that this tariff goes into operation and the hon. gentlemen know that the industries of this country are already paralyzed in consequence, while hon. gentlemen gloat, vindictively gloat over the destruction of Canadian industries. I was reading the wail, the sorrowful wail in the Montreal ' Gazette,' where one manufacturer after another declared that their industries were ruined, that their mills must close, and that they saw staring them in the face, a return to the deplorable state of things that existed when the hon. gentleman who last addressed the House was in charge of the fiscal policy of the country. I say that a deeper wrong was never inflicted on Canada.
I fancy it is not necessary for me to give the name of the speaker. The older members of the House will recognize, from the
strong language, who be was. The same speaker made another statement as to what was to happen ; but he was not wholly disheartened. He saw that some good was likely to come out of all this wreck and ruin; but he felt that the new policy would so dishearten and disgust the people of Canada that they would soon turn out the Liberal party, and return the Conservatives to power. Here Is what he said :
I feel that far from rejoicing at it, from a party standpoint, I deplore from the bottom of my heart the ruin that is going to be inflicted upon the best interests of Canada and upon its great industries. Still I hesitatingly say that from a party point of view they are doing our work, they are showing the people of this country that having obtained power, which was all they worked for, they are now prepared to use that power at the cost of the sacrifice of the industries of Canada.
This was very pathetic and very magnanimous on the part of the speaker. How his heart must have bled for poor Canada. Even the thought that the tariff as framed by the party in power was going to drive the Liberals from power and was going to be the means of placing himself and his friends once more on the treasury benches, was not sufficient to assuage the grief he felt as he thought of the battered and bruised condition in which his beloved Canada was to be left if the fiscal policy as set forth by the party in power became law. The sweets of office were nothing to him compared to the grief he felt that all these magnificent industries which had arisen all over the land under the fostering care of the national policy, were, by the iniquitous tariff now introduced, to be blighted and scattered. We had the same kind of attack on the tariff from the ex-Minister of Finance, Mr. Foster. He went more into particulars. He foresaw, with the keen sight of a seer, the complete destruction of the woollen industry, that the Canadians were to he driven out of the confectionery business, and that there was to be complete and wholesale desolation in the homes of the makers of shirts, collars and cuffs. This is what he said :
I can take Mm (Mr. Davies) down to the French constituencies in and around Montreal, and I can show him one of the most widely spread industries you will find in Canada, which is to-day distributed among hundreds and thousands of habitants, homes where the women add to the daily fare, and keep their homes by working on these articles at a moderate rate. I say that with simply an ad valorem duty that business will go to Troy or to Germany and Belgium, or to England. No person in this country feels the impost added to the cost of his shirt and collars compared at all with the derangement and destruction of an industry which goes into the homes of hundreds and thousands of people in the rural districts around the cities and villages of this country.
It seems to be a favourite pastime of some speakers to set up a man of straw in order that they may have the plensure of

knocking him down again. Tlie same speaker made a further prophecy with regard to the woollen industry.
Why should they Imperil the great and widely distributed woollen industries of this country which are spread from British Columbia to Cape Breton. My firm belief is that with five cents a pound off and only 35 per cent left on we may bid adieu to the greater part of the widely distributed woollen industry of this country.
I could keep you almost any length of time with quotations of that kind, showing you the opinions of the Conservatives of that day regarding the effects which this amended tariff would have on the destinies of the country. These are not the opinions of the rank and file of the Conservative party-that is if there be any rank and file- but of previous leaders of the Conservative party ? These are the words of Sir Charles Tapper and the hon. Mr. Foster, ex-Finance Minister, the acknowledged leader of the Conservative party. Both of these hon. gentlemen predicted that ruin and desolation were certain to come upon Canada if the Liberal party persisted in enforcing that tariff. But what positon do our hon. friends opposite take now ? The tariff in existence to-day is practically that which came into force in 1897. The same tariff which was introduced in 1897 has practically been continued down to the present day, and is the tariff which was so fiercely denounced by the Conservative party and its leaders. Has all this desolation, has all this ruin, so freely predicted, come upon the country. Why, Mr. Speaker, no one can deny that the country is prosperous. Our hon. friends opposite have to admit our prosperity, but they strive to account for it as being due to causes completely beyond the control of the government. Well, Sir, X am not one of those who say that our prosperity is due wholly to the policy of any one government. I do not think that any body on this side takes that position. I have certainly not heard any statement of the kind made in the House. But while we acknowledge that the prosperity of the country is due, in a large measure, to other causes, we also claim that there is something due to the policy and administration of the government. The fact remains at any rate, that the Liberal party are in power and that the country is prosperous, and surely the government is entitled to some credit for that condition of affairs, just as the government would be held responsible for an opposite condition. There is no lack of precedents for coming to this conclusion. Some of the older members in this House will remember the position taken by the Conservative party during the regime of the Mackenzie administration. They charged against the government all the hard times then prevailing. I cannot personally vouch for the fact, but, according to the tradition which has come down to us, they even held the Liberal government Mr. MACLAREN (Huntingdon).
of that day responsible for the plague of grass hoppers and the entrance into Canada of the potato bug. Surely then the Liberal government now in power is entitled to some credit for the prosperity we are now enjoying. In what way have they contributed to that prosperity ? They have contributed to it, Sir, by the lowering of the tariff, by the active work they have done in connection with transportation, and the good work they have done in connection with agriculture. Our agriculturists have certainly benefited to a considerable extent by the cold storage system. Of course, hon. gentlemen opposite say that that system was introduced by our predecessors, but even if it were no one can deny that it has certainly been enlarged and perfected under the administration of the present Minister of Agriculture (Hon. Mr. Fisher). It would be difficult indeed to over estimate these advantages our agricultural community at large derive from that system which enables them to put their products on the British market in perfect condition. At any rate we cannot fail to admit that the Liberals now in power, are entitled to at least as much credit for the prosperity we are enjoying as the Conservatives claim was due to themselves for the much lesser share of prosperity which prevailed during their administration. That our country is prosperous is evident by the better condition of the people, by the large increases in bank deposits, by the paying off of debts and by the general satisfaction and contentment displayed on every side. There is an old saying of that wise man, the late President Abe Lincoln, concerning the folly of swapping horses when crossing a stream, and I think that saying is particularly applicable at the present moment. It would certainly be a bad time for the country to change its fiscal policy when the country is so prosperous under conditions that now exist. These hon. gentlemen opposite are playing the pessimistic role of croakers. They are continually predicting hard times and telling us that we ought to prepare for them by reducing our expenditure. Well, some of my constituents think that the present government are too lavish in their expenditure. I myself would like to see the expenditure curtailed in some respects. However, the main thing to consider is are the expenditures made on necessary works, and do the government get good value for amount expended. In one word, Mr. Speaker, I consider the policy of this government should be to as far as possible make Canada a cheap place to live in. There is a large immigration flocking into the country ; we need more. What we want is population to occupy the vacant lands of the North-west and other parts of Canada. These immigrants are mostly persons in very straitened circumstances, and should .be able to get their implements, clothing and other manufactured articles at the lowest possible price.

It is not my intention, Mr. Speaker, to take up very muck more of your time because I have always present to my mind that mathematical calculation of my kon. friend from West Elgin (Mr. Robinson), and if I speak muck longer there will surely be a very serious charge of wasting the public money rolled up against me. But there is one other word I wish to say. A great deal has been said by hon. members opposite during the session, more particularly by the hon. member from East Grey against hon. gentlemen on the treasury benches. He said that they were nothing but procasti-nators, and that they had not performed one statesmanlike act during their whole administration.
Hear, hear.

Well, Mr. Speaker, if my hon. friend be correct in his estimate, we on this side of the House must be a poor deluded lot, far inferior to that hon. geittleman and to those who share his views. Have we really been deluded all these years in believing that we have a business administration at the head of affairs ? According to that hon. gentleman we have, but we enjoy this one consolation that we are superior in numbers, and I think, to put it mildly, equal in intelligence to himself and his friends. We have believed during all these years that we have had our country's affairs administered by the best men the country could afford. I am not saying this for the purpose of flattering hon. gentlemen on the treasury benches, but simply in vindication of myself and hon. members on this side. Is it possible that when, after the election of 1S96, the right hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier chose the members of his administration he blundered and was utterly mistaken in his choice when, in forming his cabinet, he associated with himself men who made their mark in local and Dominion politics ? And when these men, in after jmars, appealed to the country on their record and when they were approved by a large majority, I do not believe that the people were misled or deluded. I believe, on the contrary, that the estimate put by the people on these men is the correct one and not the estimate of these hon. gentlemen who sit on the other side and who speak disparagingly of those who are their superiors. I believe in praising the present government for what they have done. I believe in expressing my high opinion of the abilities of those men who have held their own with the best British and colonial statesmen and the best statesmen of the United States. Such men can well afford to be sneered at by crude and unsuccessful politicians, and we delight to honour them notwithstanding the disparaging remarks of that illustrious statesman from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) and the sneers of other hon. gentlemen opposite.
I notice the hon. gentleman (Mr. Maclaren, Huntingdon), was not good enough to tell us any one thing that they did, all the same.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to address the House,
I am conscious that the subject of debate has been already so fully discussed as to leave very little room for the introduction of new facts or new arguments to be adduced from the facts. But I avail myself of the opportunity given, of the privilege afforded, to each member of the House to place on record his views of the financial situation and of the government's policy.
I also join in the general congratulations that the country is enjoying a measure of prosperity. And, indeed, Sir, looking out on the civilized world and considering the plenty that has blessed the world during these seven years, it would be somewhat surprising if Canada did not share some of that general prosperity. I congratulate the government on the happy circumstances under which they are placed in holding the reins of power at such a time. It will be conceded on all hands by any who have given the matter attention that the reverse conditions to these-adversity, depression from whatever cause arising-have been the cause on many occasions of leaving even good governments a very precarious hold upon the confidence of the country. I say I congratulate the government as well as the country. From whatever cause our present prosperity arises, whether from the general wave of confidence throughout the civilized world with the expansion of trade resulting from it, or whether from a series of bountiful harvests, or whether, still better, it can be traced in any degree to any policy initiated and put in operation by the government-the government are to be congratulated. And, if any connection or relation can be traced between the prosperity of the country and their policy, they are welcome to all the credit they can claim and all the adulation they can crave from their supporters on that account.
But, here we may fairly ask to what extent they have changed the policy of the government which they supplanted, that policy which they had so persistently condemned before their advent to power, and which they had pledged themselves if given the power, to destroy root and branch ? What have they done towards carrying out these pledges and promises which they gave to the country ? It is true that when they came into power they gave a new name to that policy, but without importing into it any new principle. And they would now hold up that new name as sufficient to satisfy the public that they were honest in their professions and to prove that they have been consistent in their acts. But, when the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Rt. Hon. Sir Richard Cart-

Wright) tells the House and the country that the protective policy of the former government put two dollars into tlic pocket of the manufacturer or merchant for every dollar of taxation that was put into the treasury, and that the revenue tariff of this government puts every dollar of taxes into the treasury, he draws too heavily upon the credulity of the people and banks too much on his own reputation as a statesman of long and wide experience. I think it demonstrates that it is possible for a man to outlive and out-talk a fairly good reputation for honesty, consistency and good sense. If when he counsels merchants and manufacturers to avail themselves of these fat years to lay up reserves for the lean years sure to follow, to retrench, to pay off their debts if they have any while they have the revenue coming in-if he would give such advice to the government, that, while they have a buoyant revenue they should be prepared for the adverse conditions which are sure to follow, which always do follow a period of expansion and of great prosperity, if the bon gentleman would apply this advice to the government and to his own department of the government, it would perhaps redound more to his credit than making such manifestly absured statements about distinctions in tariffs which differ not at all in principle and the differences in the application of which are so infinitesimal that they are really differences in name only.
The country was led to expect a revision of the tariff this session. But, whatever, need may exist for revision the Finance Minister (Hon. Mr. Fielding) says there will be no revision at present. The government are looking at present to Great Britain for a preference in that market, and to the United States for some arrangement for a reciprocal tariff. But since the budget speech has been delivered, all hopes for British preference have been dispelled by the abolition of the corn tax. I quote from a London paper of last week as follows :
No Preference Now Possible.
The budget is remarkable also because it retraces the step which Sir Michael Hicks-Beaeh was induced to take last year alone what radical critics then called the ' slippery slope of protection.' It is far fetched to suggest that Mr. Ritchie deliberately set himself to answer the Canadian Finance Minister's threat to withdraw the British preference in the Canadian tariff, unless Canadian products shall have a preference in the British markets ; but it is quite certain that if the colonies had accepted, instead of rejecting Mr. Chamberlain's suggestions for free trade within the empire, with duties against foreigners, Mr. Ritchie would not have abolished the cereals tax from which the Canadians desired exemption. England now is on the way back to Mr. Gladstone's free breakfast table and, even if Canada refrains from withdrawing her 33 per cent preference for British goods anything like tariff unity for the empire, except on a free trade basis, is less probable than ever. In these two respects Mr. RICHARDSON.
the budget is a budget of Radicalism, not of Toryism.
Sir William Vemon-Harcourt, M. P., Liberal, said :
I am glad the grain tax has been repealed. It was an infamous impost.
air. George Toulmin, Liberal, M.P., for Bury, Lancashire, said :
The repeal of the grain duties makes it impossible for any future Chancellor of the Exchequer to initiate a preferential tariff on colonial wheat.
So, that even since this debate commenced, and since the hope expressed on the part of the Finance Minister all hopes of such an arrangement with the British government are, for the present, at an end. Any satisfactory arrangements witli the United States are equally hopeless. We have given to both Great Britain and the United States fill we have to offer in exchange for any concessions from them. To-day we stan'd with empty bands, having nothing to offer them. Our government has been one of great claims and great purposes, great promises also, but both promises and purposes have come to nought. Chasing bubbles they have grasped at nothing. A government failing so often is always changing, facing now this way and now that. This is still their condition, and they have no fixed, determined, proclaimed policy for the country, hut stand Micawber-like, waiting for something to turn up. Yet, because we are buying more goods from other countries than formerly, we are asked to jubilate that our products, and frequently our money go freely to pay for our heavy purchases in the markets of the United States and other countries.
At the opening of this debate, the House was given an instructive lesson on the wisdom and astuteness of the government in giving a preference in tariff to Great Britain without any advantage being asked in return; for while it would have been a very difficult thing to induce the British government to impose a tax on breadstuffs, exempting the colonies only, now, having given the prefernce so graciously, and Britain having since that put on a corn tax, it would be much easier for Britain to reduce that taxation by exempting the colonies from its operation. But while we are still in this debate, that hope has been dispelled, Britain has abolished her corn tax, and Canada has nothing to expect in that direction. Oh, but, say they, we can do away with our preference to Britain, and an implied threat to that effect closed the Finance Minister's speech. And so our pretended gratitude for the splendid freedom that Britain gave us will stand in history as a mean and sex-vile hypocrisy, seeking to obtain by subterfuge what a self-respecting nation should have sought for honestly, on a sound business basis. So our attitude to Britain to-day is hostile on trade l'elations.

But how do we stand with Germany ? Our relations were friendly, our trade growing, but how is it now ? We have considerable settlements of Germans, both in the older provinces and in the new territories. They form no inconsiderable portion of our best citizenship. In arts and manufactures they bring to bear that intelligence and that application that challenge competition with the world. In agricultural pursuits they are not excelled and rarely equalled by any other nationality in Canada. We want emigration from Germany, but our bungling over preferential trade with Britain has aroused such a feeling of resentment against Canada in Germany, that we are singled out of all the world as the country to which a higher prohibitive tariff must be applied. We are no longer to have the German market for our products on the same conditions as other nations. Our Finance Minister announces that we are accepting the German challenge to a tariff war; it is on now, and may embroil Great Britain as well. Our attitude to Germany is hostile.
France is another country with which we are endeavouring to cultivate better trade relations. So far our relations have been of a friendly character with that country, but now it appears from correspondence which our government has had with that country that the overtures for improved trade offered by Canada, have met with but slight response from France. Our treatment of Great Britain and our treatment by Britain, do not seem to have inspired respect for and confidence in our methods by other countries. Our relations with France, if not hostile, are not particularly amicable.
But there is our great natural market in the United States, that country that lias snubbed us at every turn; that country that deserves from us no friendship in* tariff relations, that country that has treated all our approaches to reciprocal trade with contumely and insult, the country that we were told in this House last session would never again have the opportunity of turning us down, the country towards which in future we were going to stand on our dignity-no more High Commission junketings to Washington for bettered relations; they must be the seekers not we. Wliat is our attitude to them to-day ? Why, we are informed that our government are again making their bow to Washington, and interchanging letters regarding resuming negotiations; and any needed change in our tariff must wait, wait till we see what our American friends will do for us; and possibly we may see more summer trips, pic-nics, banquets, and in the end, a big bill-that, and nothing more.
This negotiation is like chasing a bubble which, when caught, is less than nothing. Sir. Speaker, we have learned, or should have learned by this time, or long ago, that we have nothing to expect from the United States. It is not for us to be surprised that the United States statesmen should regard it a patriotic duty to trick and trip
Canada at every turn. Why should they lend their support to any policy that might by any possibility help to a more rapid development of a neighbouring state, that is destined not only to be their only rival on this continent, but will rival their supremacy in trade, commerce and manufactures in the whole world. Such, I believe to be the undoubted destiny of Canada if we be true to ourselves, and to the best interests of this country.
The first unfriendly blow given to our young commonwealth by the abrogation of the reciprocity treaty was intended in no friendly spirit for Canada. It was intended to be a knock-out blow'to the aspirations of our young nationality. I well recollect, and it must be within the memory of many members of this House, the feeling of dismay that spread through the country when it was announced that the United States had abrogated and would not renew that treaty. There were hundreds, possibly thousands of business men throughout Canada, who felt that our chances of success in competition with them were so small that we might as well, to use the common expression, throw up the sponge, that we would have no chance with them. But that which was intended to be a blow to our national aspirations proved indeed a blessing, because out of it sprung the first feeling of self-dependence, that first feeling of national sentiment which was so much needed by Canada at that time, and which is sometimes needed by Canada even at the present time. Not only then but on every subsequent occasion when we have received similar repulses from the United States, the consequence has been to strengthen and intensify that spirit of self-reliance which is a more valuable asset than the most favoured treaties could possibly be to this country. There is no fear that Americans will waste any sympathy or sentiment on Canada. We will never get any trade treaty with them, advantageous to ourselves, even though we sought for it, until they find that they need our markets. I advocate no spirit of enmity or animosity to the United States, but we have had a surfeit of such nostrums as commercial union and unrestricted reciprocity. Let us have no more coquetting with a nation ostensibly unfriendly in every trade relation with us. I would recommend the adoption of that aphorism from a popular American book, David Harum. He says : [DOT] When you go to trade hosses do to the other feller as he intends to do to you, only be sure you do it fust.' We should, as a self-respecting people, have a declared policy framed for Canada, a policy of protection for the toilers on our farms, our forests, our fisheries, for our miners and artisans in mill or shop, that there shall be for every man, as far as government can secure it, a fair return for industry and enterprise, and a certain and safe investment for capital. A weak, vacillating, uncertain, waiting policy, such as may be described in the old distich.

We can and we can't, we will and we won't,
We'll be blamed If we do, and condemned If we don't.
Is not a policy for a great, progressive country like Canada to pursue. Mr. Speaker, let us once more glance at our foreign relations-to England hostile, to Germany hostile, to France not friendly, to the United States temporizing with the only nation that merits our contempt, we are waiting for a dicker or a deal. To such humiliating conditions the present Liberal government have brought us. The United States will never give us reciprocal trade while they have our market without it, at the same time shutting us out of theirs.
But, we are told we have a big surplus. If we ask where it is we shall probably be told that it appears in the Public Accounts. But if it had any real, tangible existence, we might use the hon. Finance Minister's own argument and blame the government for taking so much more taxes from the people than they require unless it was to be used to pay off our indebtedness. It is folly to expect an uninterrupted continuity of increasing revenue any more than the increase of our population will create a corresponding increase in expenditure. I said if there be a surplus such as stated, but if it has no real existence as a convertible asset, if it is a visionary, attenuated, intangible ghost of figures created by a system of arithmetic not yet introduced or taught in the common schools, where they still believe that two and two only make four, and still believe that four from four leaves nothing, then the government have no right to take credit for it.
We are doing a large trade, but buying more than we sell. We buy from the United States ini dairy products and meats $2,550,712, and in grain $14,451,461. Our total imports of agricultural products amount to some $28,000,000 from them, and we export to the United States only $8,000,000, leaving in agricultural products alone an enormous balance of trade against Canada, our total imports from the United States in 1902 being over $129,000,000, our exports $71,000,000, leaving the total balance of trade against us nearly $50,000,000. They set up a tariff wall against our products, and it is no wonder, with such a balance of trade in their favour, that they do not wish for much change to be made in our trade relations. Just let me give a few figures illustrating the character of our relations with the United States. I have not introduced much in the way of statistics. I have avoided statistics, because so many have been quoted during the debate so far, but the few figures which I will give will not be out of place as contrasting their tariff with ours in relation to agricultural products. Against wheat they put up a tariff of 25 cents a bushel. Our tariff against their wheat is only 12 cents, the United States tariff against our oats is Mr. RICHARDSON.
15 cents, ours against theirs 10 cents, against our barley 30 cents, ours against theirs 15 cents, against our pease 40 cents, ours against theirs 10 cents, against our hay $4 per ton, ours against theirs only half that amount, $2 per ton, against our potatoes 25 cents per bushel, ours against theirs 15 cents per bushel, against our beans 45 cents per bushel, ours against theirs 15 cents, against our butter 6 cents per pound, ours against theirs 4 cents per pound. Our apples have to pay a duty of 75 cents per barrel, while theirs only pay 40 cents per barrel coming into Canada. Their tariff against our flour is 75 cents per ban-el, ours against theirs is 60 cents per barrel. Their corn comes in free, but for every bushel of corn we send to the United States there is a duty under the tariff of 15 cents. These figures illustrate the unfair trade relations existing between these two countries, and I think we can scarcely expect anything in the way of reciprocal trade while we are placed in this position. Our lonly hope for 'reciprocal trade will be in placing our tariff in such relation to theirs as to make it their necessity to seek to obtain our market by a mutual lowering of tariffs. They need our trade and our market and cannot well afford to lose them.
The expenditures of the government have been running up to an alarming extent. I do not wish to enter much into statistics, as this question has been gone over repeatedly during this debate, but I shall refer to just one item of expenditure. For immigration in 1896 the expenditure was $120,190, while in 1902 the expenditure was $494,842, an increase of $374,643. I do not complain of that increase in expenditure if the results warrant it, but I think our immigration agents have gone far afield to find settlers for the great territories now opening up for settlement and taking no note of the fact that thousands of our young men have been leaving our older provinces for the United States, and they have neither made intelligent effort to stop the drain nor replace the loss by directing the stream of immigration to the older provinces. I believe it is well that a portion of the immigration coining from the old country, and especially from Great Britain, should be absorbed by the older provinces. Farm labour is very much needed, and I believe that immigrants will more quickly become accustomed to the different life from that which they left in the old country if they settled in the older provinces, as the difference between conditions in the old country and the older provinces would not be so great as the difference between life in the old country and the western part of Canada. Had the immigration department afforded the same aids to settlement to our own people that were given to Doukhobors and others, thousands of our people who have drifted to the United States might have remained citizens of our own country. When the farm is too small
I

and will not bear further division, the necessity for change becomes pressing. It may be desirable to hold the family together, and as many people may not have the amount of money that is required to transport themselves and their families across the great distance separating the older provinces from the west, some of our annual expenditure on immigration purposes might be profitably employed in assisting the settlement of such people in the west. We need something more to bind the west to the east than railway lines and telegraph wires. We need more even than the bonds of commerce. We need the stronger bonds of sentiment and kinship, and for our farmers, compelled by growing families to move, it were infinitely better to assist them to settlement in our west than permit them through our indifference to drift across the line. I do not wish the government to enter upon a scheme of granting assistance to drain the older provinces of population, but there are individual cases where assistance might very wisely and profitably be given to settlement, assistance equal to that given to people from the older countries in Europe, who are not nearly as desirable citizens as our own Canadians are. One farmer's son from the older provinces of Canada settling in the Northwest would be worth a dozen such men as the Doukhobors, the Galicians and others.
Now, Mr. Speaker, after making these few desultory remarks I shall conclude. But let me ask : What is our attitude to-day with regard to the nations of the world. Is it that self-respecting, self-dependent position that a young country like Canada with all her wealth of natural resources with i>il the intelligence and enterprise of her citizens ; is it, I ask, that self-respecting position which Canada should occupy. Should the government of such a nation as ours have such a policy as is characteristic of the government of to-day. Should we have a waiting policy ; waiting on the wishes and whims of other countries. Should our policy not be rather a recorded policy, a pronounced policy for Canada, one that will preserve for all the citizens of Canada that fair return for labour, for enterprise, for toil, for investment that is to be found in other countries that have not the resources of Canada. It is due to ourselves, Sir, that while we shall be friendly to all, we shall be determined that we will be servile to none. I have much pleasure in supporting the amendment of the hon. leader of the opposition.

Mr. Speaker, I am a little surprised that the hon. member for South Grey (Mr. Richardson) should have in the course of his remarks, endorsed that statement credited to David Harum, that : If you are doing business with another fellow you should try and do him up. It seems to me, Sir, that this quotation applied to individuals would 62
also apply to nations if it is possible to put it into practice, and I do not think that it would be either wise or commendable to adopt the spirit of the quotation there alluded to, and endeavour to do the other fellow up. All the more is that the case when in doing so we would obtain no advantage' to ourselves. It has not surprised me, Mr. Speaker, that not alone the hon. member for South Grey (Mr. Richardson) but the majority of members on the other side, are endeavouring to depreciate as far as they can the magnificent showing that has been made in the budget speech delivered from the treasury benches. If I am not mistaken, the hon. leader of the opposition, in a speech made during the recess, when regretting the absence of a certain gentleman from this House of Commons and pleading with the people for his re-election, admitted that the opposition needed that gentleman's presence in order that they might avail of his services as a critic of the government. That admission was not very complimentary to the gentlemen who sit behind the leader of the opposition. It is equivalent to saying, that these gentlemen, able as they are, are not competent to criticise the actions of the government, or else it means that the actions of the government were so far removed from fair and honourable criticism that the opposition required some man in the House who would resort to extreme measures in order to base a criticism on the conduct of the government. That is the logic to be drawn from this statement of the leader of the opposition.
Now, Sir, while I agree with the hon. member for West Elgin (Mr. Robinson) when he stated that to a certain extent this debate had lost its interest, yet, I think there are a good many features in connection with the budget that might be emphasized. Although to a certain extent it is true that when the leaders on either side have spoken, they have said practically all that can be said on the question. I do not suppose, Sir, that I shall say anything new, and I certainly shall not say anything that will be remarkable, but I shall endeavour to try to impress upon the House one or two facts that stand out very prominently in connection with this discussion. I am satisfied that if our friends on the opposition benches had been able during any of the eighteen years they were in office, to present so magnificent a showing as has been presented by the Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding), they would have cried it from the house tops and reiterated it in black face type in all the Conservative newspapers of Canada. It seems to me. Sir. that the object of this government and of any government, should be to propound such a policy as will be for the general well-being of the country at large, and not for the wellbeing of a few manufacturers alone. And, while I do not claim that this government in its administration is entitled to all credit for the remarkably satisfactory record dur-



ing the time they have been in power, I do claim that they are entitled to some credit for it. In making that claim I am simply doing what our opposition friends did for eighteen years, because during the time they were in office, they claimed credit for any progress which was made, they - claimed credit for, and attributed it to the beneficent influences of the national policy. Now, in order to show the general prosperity of Canada, I desire to quote for the benefit of the House, and more especially for the benefit of the country, some figures in reference to our trade returns. It will be remembered that the national policy was introduced with the object of especially developing our industries and increasing our trade. In 1893, after a long experience of the national policy, our total trade reached $247,000,000, which was the highest it ever reached during the Conservative regime. In 1896 our total trade was only $239,000,000. During the twenty-three years preceding this, our total trade had only increased by a little over $60,000,000, or an average of less than $3,000,000 a year. Be it remembered that during all that time we had what our friends on the other side of the House called a policy of adequate protection. We had what they believed to be a policy of sufficient protection; what they believed to be the highest perfection so far as legislation is concerned, that could contribute to the well-being and advancement and prosperity of the country. How well the national policy accomplished that, or how well it failed, may be shown by comparing our trade returns during the Conservative administration with our trade returns during the Liberal regime. In 1896, as I have said, the total trade of Canada amounted to $239,000,000. The Liberals had no sooner taken hold of the reins of office ; they were no sooner installed apparently, than our trade began to advance at a marvellous rate. Here is the record :

I have given these figures in round numbers, and they show that during the six years of Liberal government, our total trade increased by $163,000,000. Now, our total trade for the current year shows an increase along the same lines, which increase will probably amount to $40,000,000, so that the total increase for the seven years of the Liberal government will amount to $200,000,000, or an average yearly increase of nearly $30,000,000. I am not surprised that in the face of these figures our friends on

the opposite side should endeavour to underestimate the prosperity which this country is enjoying. I am not surprised that they should endeavour to explain away as far as they can, the prosperity which exists and attribute it alone to the general prosperity prevailing all over the world. I am not prepared to admit, Sir, that our prosperity is due solely to the fact that other nations are prosperous. If we accept that as a suitable argument we are thrown back upon the proposition :	That during the eighteen
years the Conservatives were in power the other nations of the world were'not making that progress which they relatively should, and it also follows, that this policy of protection in which the Conservatives place so much confidence now, did not produce the good results which they claimed it would during the years they were in power. Nor am I surprised that the gentlemen on the other side of the House endeavour to underestimate and depreciate the remarkable financial record which was proclaimed in the speech of the Minister of Finance. Had our Conservative friends been able to show the very large surpluses which the Liberal government have been able to show, they would have extolled it as a renewed evidence of the statesmanlike policy of their party. When the Conservatives were in power they claimed credit for all the good things that were going. Not only did they claim credit for the prosperity of the country, but they claimed credit whenever they had a surplus. They did not claim credit for having deficits, but while they were responsible for the surpluses, nevertheless they left the deficits out of the reckoning when they were glorifying themselves. I have here some figures which have already been submitted to the House, but they will bear repetition. They say that a good story cannot be told too often, and acting upon that principle, I desire to submit some figures bearing on our present financial standing.
In 1896-97, the Liberals, on entering office, having assumed certain responsibilities and obligations which had been incurred by their predecessors, found themselves face to face with a deficit of $519,000. In the following year they had a surplus of nearly $2,000,000, in 1898-9 they had a surplus of nearly $5,000,000, in 1899-1900, a surplus of $8,000,000, in 1901-2 a surplus of $7,000,000, and this year they will have an estimated surplus of $13,350,000, or a total surplus in the seven years of nearly $41,000,000. The average annual surplus during the seven years of the Liberal administration has been $5,569,275, while the average annual surplus during the eighteen years of Liberal-Conservative rule-and our Liberal-Conservative friends used to boast upon the housetops and everywhere else of the great success of their administration-amounted to $544,000. Now, I am not specially concerned about the increase of the debt. I think the people of this country will not

quarrel with the administration about any increase of debt provided it is a legitimate increase, by virtue of the construction of various public works of a productive character, and provided that the money is properly and honestly expended, as it is under the Liberal administration. Our friends on the opposition benches may naturally take exception to an increased expenditure ; but they have been unable so far to point to any expenditure that has not been in the general interest of the country at large ; and I am satisfied that the people will endorse an increased expenditure so long as it is consistent with the development of the country, and in its best interests. But there is this fact to be borne in mind, which would have afforded unbounded glory to hon. gentlemen opposite if they had been able to report it in their time, that there has been an actual reduction of $5,000,000 in the debt of the country. The government has carefully looked after all t}ie public works required and the various matters calling for expenditure, not only without any increase in the public debt, but with an actual reduction of the debt.
Now, our friends on the opposite side of the House have taken the members on this side and the government to task for having no declared policy on the question of protection. I have listened to almost all the speeches which have been delivered by members on the other side of the House, and so far I have failed to hear any specific declaration as to what they think should be the amount of protection afforded to the various industries of the country. They do not define it in their resolution. They state that there should be some declared policy of adequate protection. Members on this side have asked the hon. leader of the opposition himself as well as those who follow him, to define or specify what they mean by a declared policy of adequate protection, and so far no member on the other side of the House has given any definition thereof. As a matter of fact, the amendment before the House is a negative amendment, because it proposes actually nothing at all. It simply states that there should be adequate protection ; but none of the hon. gentlemen opposite apparently are able or willing to state what in their opinion may be regarded as adequate protection. What might be adequate protection for one industry might not be for another, and what might be Adequate protection in the mind of one member might not be adequate protection in the mind of another. Therefore you may realize the difficulty of _ arriving at a definite conclusion upon an indefinite term of that kind, in the absence of anything specific In the resolution. Looking over our tariff, I find that it runs all the way from 20 to 40 per cent; and it seems to me that a tariff offering 40 per cent or even 35 per cent protection should be sufficient under normal conditions for our manufacturers. It simply means that if a manufacturer under ordinary conditions produces and places on the market $100 worth of goods, the present tariff, which our lion, friends say is not adequate, enables him to charge for those goods $135. It gives him an advantage of $35, which it seems to me should be sufficient for all practical purposes, and I am not one of those who think that this protection should be increased very materially. I notice that I am quoted by the hon. leader of the opposition as being a protectionist. In his speech he did me the honour of including me with some others as being in favour of protection. Well, Mr. Speaker, I assume that we are all more or less protectionists, according to local circumstances or conditions ; but as to being a protectionist in the ordinary sense of the term I have to deny the soft impeachment. I am not a protectionist, but, I believe in freedom of trade, so far as wp can have it consistently with the needs of our revenue.
As to the marvellous development which has taken place in the trade of the country under the Liberal regime, our friends of the opposition claim that that is due to worldwide prosperity-that it is. because there is prosperity in all other nations. We might ask, what is the reason that other nations of the world are enjoying prosperity ? I think they will find, if they inquire, t*at the reason is not because of an artificial system of protection, which would go to the upbuilding of manufactures, but that it may be-I will not say must be-due to natural causes. If it be true that the prosperity of other lands is largely due to natural causes-and I believe that is the case in the United States-while our friends opposite cite the United States as an example of the benefits of a highly protective policy, they forget that within themselves the United States, are a free trade people. Having various kinds of climate, and soil, they are not in a position to be compared to the Dominion of Canada. But if it be true that the prosperity of the world is due to natural causes, and that the general progress and prosperity of Canada is due to the same causes, then I contend that it is the duty of this government, as far as lies in its power, to look to the development of our natural resources, whereby we may increase the wealth of the country. Hon. gentlemen opposite want that to be done by a higher tariff. I believe it can be done by a lower tariff. I believe that it has been done by a lower tariff, and if we seek to develop our natural resources, as far as we can, without putting oppressive burdens on the people, it will be better for the prosperity of our own country. The hon. member for North Grey referred to the action of the government.
It is South Grey and not North Grey.

said regarding the question of reciprocity with the United) States, I am in favour of reciprocity provided we can get it on fair and honourable terms. I cordially agree in the opinion expressed by the right hon. the leader of this House when he said :	I
think it was in the city of Quebec-that the Dominion would never again go to Washington and get down on its knees and ask for reciprocity. But while that statement meets with my fullest approval, I am iu favour of securing reciprocity on fair and equitable terms. I have the assurance of manufacturers to-day that, if the American market were thrown open to them they would not fear the competition of the manufacturers of that country, but that they are perfectly willing to enter the American market if they are given access thereto-

speechtext:
Hear, hear.
Mr. HOLMES-And that statement, I take it, is endorsed by my hon. friend from Leeds (Mr. Taylor)-
But will the American market ever be thrown open to our manufacturers ? Until it is, we have a right to look after our own.

My hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) may be correct, or he may not. But he must bear in mind that, for all time to come, we remain the neighbour of the country to the south of us; and so, for all time to come, we should try to secure the most workable and favourable trade relations with them that it is possible for us to secure. Our destinies may not be bound up with theirs, and yet, to a certain extent we are one nation, speaking the same tongue. And I do not wish anybody to assume from what I say that I am in favour of annexation, for I am not in favour of that at all. During visits I have made to our American friends, when opportunities have presented themselves on public occasions, I have publicly repudiated the idea that any feeling in favour of annexation exists in this country. I do not believe that any such feeling exists, but I believe a strong feeling exists in favour of good trade relations with our neighbours to the south. And I say that, situated as we are, it would be almost-suicide, I was going to say that that would be rather a strong term, perhaps, but it would certainly not be in our best interests to erect a high tariff wall between ourselves and our neighbours to the south. Our friends on the other side of the House advocate the erection of a Chinese wall. They would have us trade absolutely within ourselves. Anybody who knows anything about trade knows that that would be impossible.
If we were able to secure concessions from our friends to the south-and the indications point that way notwithstanding what my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) says-it would be in the interest of Canada for the government to entertain any proposition looking to that end. I listened to the hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) the other night, and was more than surprised that a man living in the neck of land that my hon. friend lives in, the south-western part of Ontario, should take the stand that he took in opposition to closer trade relations with the United States. He has a right to his opinion, as X have a right to mine, but I have conversed with many men who live in that section and have come in contact with a large number of them, and I say without fear of successful contradiction-a man may contradict and yet not contradict successfully-that that neck of land lying west of the city of I.ondon, if we had closer trade relations with the United States, would increase in prosperity, and its land would rise in value to a marvellous extent. Hon. gentlemen opposite seek to make it appear that we have no trade with the United States, or rather that we are buying from the United States and not selling to them. The hon. member for South Grey (Mr. Richardson) quoted the American tariff to show that their tariff was higher on certain lines than ours, and therefore it was wiser for us not to seek better trade relations with them or to do business with them. There is no force in saying that their duty on grain is 25 cents a bushel while ours is lower. It would make no difference if their duty were 50 cents a bushel-it would not affect the price of the Canadian farmers' grain, and, those hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House who are farmers, know that this is true. But, to show the House and the country that we do trade with the United States notwithstanding their hostile tariff-which trade would be larger, then, if they had not a hostile tariff-I wish to quote a few figures. These relate to agricultural products, and they are not all the figures that might be quoted. Hon. gentlemen opposite never tire of seeking to convince the House that our farmers suffer by the competition of the people to the south of us. The fact is that there are no articles that have been mentioned that come into competition with the articles produced by the Canadian farmer. The figures I shall quote show the exports from Canada to the United States of certain articles notwithstanding the high rate of duty they have to pay :
Horned cattle, year old, $124,497, duty of $2 per head ; horned cattle, over year old, $699,178, duty of $3.75 per head ; horses, $652,303,duty of $30 per head ; sheep, year old or less, $803,701, duty of $1.50 per head ; sheep, over year old, $118,436, duty of $1.75 per head ; swine, $81,516, duty of $1.50 per head ; poultry, $55,862, duty of 3 cents per pound live, 5 cents dressed; animals, all told, living, $2,535,493.

Barley, $9,499, duty 30 cents per bushel- (Dingley) ; beans, $185,921, duty 45 cents per bushel ; buckwheat, $2,141, 15 cents per bushel; oats, $62,322, 15 cents per bushel ; pease, $145,102 ; grain, all told, $446,712.
So, we sell living animals to the value of over two millions of dollars notwithstanding that onr American friends are producers of the very class of stock that we produce. It will be seen from the figures that we find very little market now in the United States for our barley. That market was nearly cut off by the Dingley tariff-nobody disputes that. The beans, of which we sent $183,000 worth, notwithstanding the duty of 45 cents per bushel, were the product, very largely, of the province of Ontario, and of that section of it represented by my hon. friend from Bothwell, a section which, he intimated, would receive no advantage from reciprocity with the United States.
