speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman furnish me with the statistics ?

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor) can have them and welcome. Some I got from the American returns and some from our own. I declare myself in favour of reciprocal trade relations with our neighbours to the south. I say I am in favour of it because I believe that it would aid to the well-being and advancement of this country. I am glad that our government has taken the wise step of either lowering the duties or taking off the duties upon certain articles of the produce of the United States. I think the present government have conferred no greater benefit upon the farmers of the Dominion of Canada than by taking off entirely the duty on corn. Notwithstanding what has been said by hon. gentlemen opposite, I am satisfied that the government conferred an inestimable boon upon the farmers when they removed that duty, and I am satisfied that that opinion is held by the farmers of the Dominion irrespective of their political predilections.
Does the hon. gentleman think that the Western Ontario peninsula, of which he has spoken, will endorse that ?

I feel sure that the section of which my hon. friend (Mr. Clancy) is one of the representatives will endorse it, for the reason that the corn that comes in does not enter into competition, to any appreciable extent, with the corn grown in the district represented by my hon. friend. I have had Conservatives come to me, men of pronounced political convictions, men who have no sympathy with this government but have done everything they possibly could to prevent the return of its supporters-I have had these men come to me and endorse in unqualified terms the action of the government in removing the duty on corn. I have heard them commend the government because of its attitude on this matter, declaring that if in no other respect the government was worthy of commendation, it was worthy of commendation in this. What does it do, Mr. Speaker ? It enables the Canadian farmer, to a greater extent than he ever could under former conditions, to finish his Canadian cattle and to put them on the English market in competition with his American friends, almost upon equal footing. The hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) knows perfectly well-he poses as a farmer while I do not-that the Canadian farmer was handicapped in the fact that he was compelled to fall back upon his own coarse grains for feeding his stock, and therefore it cost him more to feed his stock than it would, under ordinary conditions, if he could have secured American corn. There are years when he cannot secure American corn, when it is too high, and it may be more profitable for him to use his own coarse grain. But the Canadian farmer knows to-day that it has paid him better to sell his coarse grains in the open market, and buy corn for the purpose of finishing his cattle, which he can then send to the English market in competition with the American farmer. My hon. friend may laugh; but I am prepared at any time to go on any platform in the country, and face him in advocacy of that position. Then I say that I am in hearty sympathy with the idea of obtaining reciprocal trade with our neighbours to the south of us, assuming, of course, that it is possible to get it. If it is not possible to get it, then I would do the best I could in the development of our own interests in some other direction. But I think it would be to the advantage of the Dominion at large to have reciprocal trade relations with the United States, to some extent at any rate.
Fault has been found and is found with our immigration policy. But it does not lie in the mouths of our hon. friends on the opposite side of the House to point to what they claim to be the shortcomings or defects of our immigration policy. We know that the policy pursued by hon. gentlemen opposite did not enable them to get immigrants to come to this country, at least we know in how few numbers they came

when hon. gentlemen opposite were in power. On the other hand, whether it is due to the marvellous prosperity and progress of this country or not, immigrants are now coming in by the thousands and tens of thousands. Moreover, our Conservative frieds say, why does not the government take more interest in Canadians and do something for Canadians instead of spending their time and money on foreigners ? Why did not our hon. friends do it when they were in power themselves ?
That is no argument.

It may not be a very good argument. The hon. member for Toronto does not regard it as a good argument because it happens to hit his own party in a tender spot. If the argument is good in the one instance, if it is right now that the government should pay special attention to Canadians, it was right during the eighteen years when our friends opposite were in power; and they should be honest and candid enough to acknowledge that they did not do during those eighteen years what they claim now we ought to do. I say this, Mr. Speaker, that while I am perfectly willing that the government should do its utmost for Canadians who are within our land, and while I believe firmly that Canadians would make better settlers in the North-west than quite a few who are now coming from foreign lands, still I am not hostile to foreign immigrants, a term that I suppose will embrace the Doukhobors and Galicians, and men of that kind. I have conversed with people in the North-west, as I presume some of my hon. friends opposite have done, in reference to the Doukhobors, and notwithstanding their mistake of last year-and for that I think they are perhaps entitled to a certain amount of consideration in view of their circumstances-the people of the Northwest will tell you that there are no better settlers, taking them all around, there is no community in the North-west that gives better promise for the future than the Doukhobors.
All bosh.

Perhaps it is all bosh. The hon. member for Halton knows how easy it is to say, it is all bosh. But that is no argument. As the hon. member for Toronto said himself a moment ago, that is no argument. My hon. friend who makes that remark cannot go into any town in the North-west adjacent to a Doukhobor settlement, and repeat the ejaculation that he throws across the floor of this House.
I made no remark at all about the Doukhobors.
I did not allude to the hon. gentleman.
He said the member for Toronto.
I alluded to the hon. member for Halton, who was using an argument similar to that which had just been used by the member for Toronto.
I did not interrupt the hon. gentleman by a single word.
I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon, I thought it was he who made the remark.
There was a good deal of bosh in what he said, but I did not interrupt him.

I am sorry to attribute to the hon. gentleman any views he does not hold, I accept his disclaimer, and I hope he will have the forbearance to accept my apology. When two or three members opposite are making ejaculations it is not always easy to tell where they come from. But I do not wish intentionally to wound the feelings of the hon. member for Halton, and if he did not make the remark some other hon. member opposite did make it. I think the present government is entitled to commendation for its immigration policy. In order to develop our country we want population, and if we can get population of a more or less desirable kind, I think the government is entitled to credit therefor. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, to be a picayune policy indeed to take exception to this, that, or the other nationality who are coming here, although in due course of time they will no doubt take the oath of allegiance and become good Canadian citizens, just as good as any other people we have. If we go back to the history of this country we will find that it has been settled by men of different nationalities, Germans, Irish, Scotch, and perhaps some heathen. But in course of time they have developed into good, industrious and reputable Canadian citizens. I do not tbink it becoming in hon. gentlemen opposite to throw stones in the way they do at the different nationalities. I have no special love for any particular nationality, but when they come to our shores and assume the responsibilities of citizens, and take their due part in building up this country, they are entitled to every credit and consideration.
Now what should the government do for Canadians ? How many Canadians are there who go to the North-west who would be willing to accept government aid and government assistance, even to the limited extent that we give it to those who come to us from foreign shores ? Very few Canadians indeed. The spirit of independence in the heart of Canadians is so strong that they are unwilling to accept what may be for the time being reasonable assistance in order to help them move their homes to other portions of the Dominion. But I say that the Dominion government to-day offers the very same facilities to any residents of the older provinces that they offer to residents

of foreign lands. There is no hindrance whatever to native Canadians obtaining for themselves a home in the North-west; they have the very same privilege which is given to incoming immigrants.
Now, Mr. Speaker, reference is made In that resolution to the protection of the farmer as well as to protection of the labourer. Some hon. gentlemen opposite have tried to convince the House, though it seemed to me they were arguing against their own convictions, that they believed in a policy that could protect the farmer. Well, the protection that the farmer can get from any policy of adequate protection or from the indefinite protection advocated by the hon. gentlemen opposite, is so infinitesimally small that, to use a common phrase, it does not amount to a hill of beans. The farmers were hoodwinked in Canada once by the promise of increased protection. A man came into my office immediately after the adoption of the national policy and he said to me : ' We are going to have a higher price for our wheat now.' I said : ' I am glad to know that you are going to have a higher price for your wheat. How are you going to get a higher price.' He said :	'We have the national
policy and it is going to give us a higher price.' I asked : ' How are we going to get it ?' ' Why,' he said with confidence in his face, ' Didn't Sir John go over to' the old country and arrange, himself, that they should give us a higher price for our grain ?' He went away with the conviction that Sir John, the old hero and chieftain of our hon. friends opposite, had actually arranged with the authorities of the mother country that they should pay a higher price for our grain. Our hon. friends opposite know that it is absolutely impossible to protect the farmer. They know perfectly well, notwithstanding their own statements, that no matter how high we put the tariff it cannot protect the farmer, because, when the farmer is compelled to find a market for his products in the market of the world, his products are subjected to the competition of the world, and no amount of protection can remedy that condition. What the government can do, what the government has done, and what the government desires to do, is to relieve as far as possible the burdens that were oppressive so far as the farmers are concerned, and in this way it is doing everything possible to promote the development and prosperity of the country. Then, I would like to ask our hon. friends to define, or declare in some specific way, how they are going to protect the labourer of this country. The labourer was once misled. He thought that if the national policy was adopted, as it was adopted, he would enjoy a larger measure of prosperity than ever before. Yet, the experience of the labouring classes was not in harmony with that belief. Under the policy which we have at the present time, under the policy condemned by our hon. friends opposite, under the policy

which they say does not give the manufacturer his home market and does not contribute to the prosperity of the mechanics and labouring classes generally, there is such a demand for skilled labour that not long ago a lot of men in the city of Toronto went to the Ontario government, a thing that never occurred during the eighteen years' regime of our Conservative friends, and asked the government if they could not make some arrangement whereby additional skilled labour could be brought to this country. They said they could not get enough skilled labour, that the demand is so great, that under this policy, as was stated by the hon. member for Huntingdon (Mr. Mae-Laren), at the present time the industries are so thriving, so prosperous, that they cannot secure the amount of labour that they require at the present time. There is undoubtedly a great demand for skilled labour. But, my hon. friends opposite say that the government has done nothing, that we are not enjoying any marked prosperity, but at the same time they want to introduce a policy which would take the labourer from one class of labour and put him possibly at another, while there is a greater demand for skilled labour as compared with unskilled labour than there has been at any previous time in the history of Canada. One speaker on the other side of the House, I think the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) In his eulogy, made the statement that a lot of the credit was due to the splendid national policy that was introduced eighteen years ago and established by the present, opposition when they were in power. He said that a great deal of our prosperity was due to that fact. Well, if the prosperity that we enjoyed, such as it was, was due to the national policy, the prosperity we are enjoying now, such as it is, is also due to the administration of affairs at the present time. One is as logical an argument as the other. Then we are told that we ought to manufacture every dollar's worth of goods that we import at the present time. This is an important statement, but it is no argument, because, if we manufactured evei'y dollar's worth of goods we import now we would have to resort to direct taxation for revenue or raise the revenue in some other way and, therefore, the policy we are pursuing at the present time is the best policy that we can pursue in harmony with the existing state of affairs. I was glad to notice that the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir Richard Cartwright), in his admirable speech the other night, brought out the fact that the development of the foreign trade of this country amounted to 96 per cent, while the development of the foreign trade of the United States only amounted to 46 per cent, which in itself is a contradiction of the position taken by hon. gentlemen opposite. I do not want to take up the time of the House, because I am simply going over matters that have been gone over

before, but if necessary X could go through the various departments and show the excellence of the administration in connection with these departments which has contributed to the general prosperity and general well-being of the country. I am not surprised that our lion, friends opposite sometimes almost turn green with envy at the magnificent showing that lias been made in the different departments. Take the Post Office Department, the Railways and Canals Department, the Department of Agriculture and any other department that you might name and you will find that the administration has been far superior in its results at any rate to that in vogue under the regime of our hon. friends opposite, and the results have been so striking that I am not at all surprised that they endeavour to minimize them as much as possible. But, the people of the country who are intelligent, notwithstanding the misrepresentations which may be thrown abroad at different times, know perfectly well that we are not alone enjoying prosperity, but that we are enjoying a greater degree of prosperity in the various departments than under the old regime. It was said by the hon. member foist. Mary's, Montreal (Hon. Mr. Tarte), and it has been stated by speakers on the other side of the House, that no country can be prosperous with a large balance of trade against it. When the hon. gentleman made that statement and supported it by figures without end, our friends on the other side of the House applauded the statement as if it were a fact. What is the fact ? If no country can be prosperous with a large balance of trade against it, will our hon. friends opposite tell me how it is that Great Britain has always had a balance of trade against it ? The balance of trade has been against Great Britain for almost all time and if the argument used by the hon. member for St. Mary's, Montreal, and endorsed warmly and applauded by hon. members opposite, be true, then Great Britain must be almost in a state of national bankruptcy. We know that to be entirely contrary to the fact. If hon. gentlemen opposite want to look at a country where there is disclosed, perhaps, the logical results of a high tariff, they have simply to look at Germany, where they will find a state of affairs existing which is one we would not like to copy in this country. I do not think the labouring classes or the farming classes in Germany are enjoying that measure of prosperity that we have been enjoying. Germany has a high protective tariff, but it has not the prosperity which hon. gentlemen opposite claim we would have if we adopted that tariff. My hon. friend from South Brant (Mr. Heyd) informs me that it has a large balance of trade against it; therefore, it cannot be prosperous. There are one or two other matters I want to allude to and then I shall take my seat. I agree with the hon. member for Aiberta (Mr. Oliver) in one respect, that the government might have gone farther
than it did so far as the reduction of the tariff is concerned. I do not know why the tariff on coal oil is kept on. It is a small amount. It does not look to be very large. It is true that the government has reduced it and I think they were wise in reducing it. I do not know perhaps that it would make very much difference if the duty was taken off altogether so far as the price is concerned to the consumer, under the existing circumstances. But insignificant ns the item may appear, there are a good many people in rural sections especially who wish to see the duty taken off coal oil. I would have been glad had the government seen its way clear to do what apparently would have been in the interests of the consumer, and I do not know that any existing industry in Canada at the present time -would have suffered in connection therewith.
I stated at the outset of my remarks that all men were more or less protectionists according to local considerations and conditions. I stated that on general principles I believe in freer trade, though not absolute free trade, because we can not have free trade. And yet at the same time, I am to a certain extent a protectionist. There may be exceptional cases in which protection would be advisable-I use the term in a qualified sense. Sometimes I have thought that hon. members on the other side of the House produced strong cases for exceptional treatment, and the government apparently took that view in connection with some of its own legislation. Notwithstanding the fact that the government stands for tariff reform or a tariff for revenue, (and a tariff for revenue is protective to that extent at any rate), the government took the view that on certain lines they would be justified in increasing or readjusting the tariff. They may be right; I will not say they are wrong. To that extent I am a protectionist, and I am a protectionist by virtue of local surroundings and circumstances-
What were these articles?
I do not call them to mind at the moment, but it did suggest itself to me when I heard some of these gentlemen opposite speaking.
Salt for example ?

I am going to allude to salt. Even at the risk of my bon. friend calling me inconsistent, I think I can show that the tariff on salt is not just what it ought to be, and I will point out to my hon. friend and to the House why I think so.
Hear, hear.

The government thinks that special treatment should be accorded to beet root sugar. That may be right and it may be wrong. I am not a very strong supporter of the beet root sugar argument, because I am a little inclined to think that I we will never be able to successfully es-

tablish a beet root sugar industry in this country, unless it is done by subsidies or bonuses or something of that kind. X think that is the experience of our friends on the other side of the line, and I am not satisfied in my own mind that the beet root sugar industry can lie permanently established here. If it can, well and good. If we can make it a permanent success without it costing our people too much, then I am not prepared to find much fault with it. But, if we believe in a tariff for revenue as we advocate, then I say that the tariff should be so adjusted as to produce the revenue that is necessary. Then the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) called attention to the circular placed in the hands of members of this House by a Arm representing the salt industry in my own town-it not only represents the salt industry in my own town but it largely represents the salt industry in the province of Ontario. Because all the salt industries in the province of Ontario are under the direction of two or three individuals, and one of these firmg has its office in my own town. Now, the government believes it was wise and prudent to extend special consideration to the beet root sugar industry.
In what way ?
In providing especially that machinery might lie introduced free of duty in connection with the beet root sugar industry.
A great concession, that.

Nevertheless it is a concession, whether it is great or otherwise. The government took the same view with regard to steel rails. I presume that my hon. friend (Mr. Clancy) with equal force and logic will say that that is a great concession also. At any rate the government took the ground that with reference to steel rails certain consideration should be shown to the manufacturers of steel rails.
AVhat do you think of putting a duty on steel rails ?
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) would like to lead me astray by drawing a herring across the track.
Hear, hear.

I am a little afraid that the duty on steel rails will not turn out in the end as some of the gentlemen on the other side think it will. That is my opinion with reference to steel rails. At the present time the manufacturers of salt have a duty of seven and a half cents per hundred on salt in packages, and five cents per hundred pounds on salt imported in bulk. The manufacturers of salt would not find fault with that if they were not handicapped in a way in which perhaps other industries are not handicapped. It is not for me to advise the government as to its trade policy, but while others have expressed their opinion on this side of the House, I presume that I may ex-Mr. HOLMES.
press my opinion also. I think it would have been a wise thing on the part of the government to have met our American friends in the matter of the remission of the duty on coal. AVhere the Americans have taken the duty off coal I think it would have been a wise thing on the part of this government to remove our duty on coal. I believe it would have been a concession to the manufacturers all over the Dominion. It would have been equivalent to a certain amount of protection, and to that extent the salt manufacturers think that it would have been especially to their advantage had the duty on coal been removed. The salt manufacturers are handicapped in this way : they do not complain alone about the competition from the United States, but they also object to the competition from the old country, and they claim, I think with a great degree of force, that believing as we do in a tariff that shall be a revenue producing tariff, there should be a tariff upon salt the same ns there is upon any other article. Binder twine was singled out by the government for special consideration, and the government takes to itself power to deal with binder twine in case they find it advisable and necessary to do so.
No, they do not.

Our salt manufacturers complain of two things. They complain of the free importation of English salt, and they complain generally of the importation of American salt. The English salt comes in here free of duty by virtue of being used in the fisheries, and if you take the returns of trade and commerce you will find that it is not alone imported from Great Britain but it is also imported to a certain extent from the United States under this head. The manufacturers of salt think that when they are handicapped by taxes of various kinds, that English salt manufacturers should be placed in the same category as they are, and should contribute a certain amount to the revenue of this country. They do not see why even the maritime fisheries should enjoy the benefits of free salt, while people in the upper provinces are called upon to pay an increase cost by virtue of the tariff if they import salt. If the English salt was used for the fisheries alone, there would not be so much force in my argument in asking for a duty upon it, but unfortunately for the manufacturers of Canadian salt, English salt also enters into commercial competition, because it comes westward and is sold in competition with Canadian salt. To that extent the Canadian manufacturers are handicapped in that direction and are unfairly and unjustly dealt with.
Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) For whose benefit ?

Presumably for the benefit of the fishermen of the lower provinces.
Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) Yes, and for the farmers also.

Of course, if my bon. friend assumes that position he should throw the duties off entirely, and make all things equal. But the salt manufacturers are called on first of all to pay a duty on coal which amounts to the equivalent of 4 cents on every barrel of salt. That may seem to be a small amount, but when they manufacture a great quantity of salt any one can see that in the aggregate it would amount to a great deal. The salt manufacturers are exceptional with respect to their use of coal, for there is no industry which I am aware of in the prosecution of which it requires such a large quantity of coal to produce a given amount of manufactured goods as it does in the manufacture of salt. The coal tax presses particularly heavy on the salt manufacturers, because it takes a ton of coal at least to make two tons of salt. I do not think a similar condition prevails in any other line of manufacture. Our salt manufacturers ask, and with a certain degree of reason and force, that our tariff should at least be made equal to the American tariff, or if not, that it should be logically called a revenue producing tariff, because the English salt, which comes in and enters into competition with Canadian salt, should bear a share of the burden which the latter has to bear. The salt manufacturers are also taxed for their bags, taxed on iron, and on a variety of articles used in connection with their business. It seems to me, free trader as I may be, that there is a great amount of force in the contention that our salt manufacturers are unjustly dealt with by being taxed on their raw material while they are not in a position to compete on equal terms with foreign producers. Our American friends have this advantage, that they are endeavouring to force the small manufacturers of the United States into a large combine, and, in order to do that, are selling salt at low prices. The Americans have the further advantage of cheaper transportation than we have in Canada. In all these respects our salt manufacturers are placed at a disadvantage, and for the reasons stated I think are deserving of consideration at the hands of the government.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have said practically all I want to say. I say unhesitatingly that the general policy pursued by the present administration is a policy that very largely meets with my approval and endorsation, not simply because I sit on this side of the House, but because it seems to me to be the policy best adapted to promote the development of the country at large, and the interests of all classes of our people! Somebody has said-I think it was my hon. friend from South Brant (Mr. Heyd), with whom in private conversation I have sometimes a controversy on these questions-that this country should not be an agricultural or pastoral country. On this point there is one fact that must be borne in mind. We may develop our manufacturing industries to the fullest extent
possible, whether by virtue of the development of our lands or by virtue of increased protection ; but, first and foremost, this country must be for all time an agricultural country. We cannot help it. Let any man travel over the Dominion of Canada, from the Atlantic on the east to the Pacific on the west, and he will come to but one conclusion, that with the large agricultural area which we possess, and the vast extent of territory yet undeveloped which must inevitably come under the farmer's hand, we must first of all give attention to the development of our agricultural interests ; and with the development of these will come the development of our manufacturing interests. One is a sequence of the other. Therefore, I contend that it is our duty first and foremost to see to the well-being and prosperity of the largest class in the community. The farmers are by all odds the largest class ; and if by legislation, or in any other way, we can contribute to the prosperity of that class, if we can make two blades of grass grow where only one grew before, it is our duty to do so. Then and then only will come the true and solid development of our manufacturing industries-a development that will stand for all time to come. We have a noble heritage ; we have a grand country, and I am glad to see that hon. members on both sides of the House wish it to develop and prosper. Unfortunately, we are not all of the same opinion as to how that development and prosperity can be best brought about. There is no reason why we should not agree to differ on questions of policy ; but in our legislation and in whatever action we take, we should have in view the interest and the welfare of the masses and not the classes, of those who bear the burden and heat of the day, of those who sweat and toil, of those who are not in the fortunate circumstances of the men who have the advantage of protection, of those who have not as luxurious homes or as many of the luxuries and comforts of life as most of our manufacturers. I do not say that this is true of them all ; but relatively speaking, the manufacturers enjoy a greater degree of wealth and prosperity than the farmers, and I do not say this in any way as reflecting upon this important class in the community, but it is the duty of this House to legislate in such a way as to contribute to the development and wellbeing of the greatest body in the community.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, representing, as I do, one of the largest agricultural constituencies in the province of Ontario, I think I am simply doing my duty in voicing what I believe to be the opinions of the large majority of my constituents. Before I address myself particularly to the budget speech made by the hon. Minister of Finance, and to the amendment thereto moved by the hon. leader of the opposition, I want to say a few words in regard to the speech which has just been

delivered by the hon. member for West Huron (Mr. Holmes). That hon. gentleman has travelled north by south, east by west. He Is a protectionist, a free trader, a revenue tariff man ; anything that the government may adopt he will follow and cheerfully support. He quotes a number of statistics of agricultural products which he claims are exported to the United States for home consumption ; but in the short time that I have had to look into the matter, I am satisfied that the great majority of these exports have been bought by speculators and exported in bond through the United States to other foreign countries. Then, in discussing the position of the manufacturers in this country, he told us that one of them had said to him that he would be quite willing, if the United States would throw down their tariff wall, to meet the American manufacturers on fair ground. I am satisfied that that statement is tine. The hon. gentleman cannot find in this country a manufacturer who would not be willing to meet the United States manufacturers in a fair field, but he is not willing to meet them with one hand tied behind his back, as he is by the Canadian tariff being so much lower than the American. But give us a fair field, and the manufacturers of Canada are prepared to meet those of the United States in the open market. So are our farmers ; but we do not want the United States to be pouring their free corn into this country when we have to pay duty in the United States on the grains which the free corn displaces. My hon. friend asked : How are we going to protect the farmers of this country ? The farmers, in my opinion, are fairly well protected now, thanks to the Conservative government and the National Policy. Let me point my hon. friend to one industry which has grown up in this country within a few years. I was the first one in this House, I think it was in 1885, to advocate the placing of a duty upon pork. I proved to the government that in the year previous we had imported into this country $12,000,000 worth of pork, beef, and the products of beef and pork. I asked the government to come down with a protective tariff on pork, and I predicted that in a very few years this country, in place of sending $12,000,000 to the United States for beef and pork, would be raising plenty to "feed our own people and have a large export beside. We used to send $12,000,000 to the United States for pork and beef with which to feed the people of this country, and when the pork and beef was gone the Americans had our money and the Canadians had nothing but the bone and muscle which that beef and pork produced. The late government came down with a protective tariff on those articles. and what has been the result ? Every farmer in Canada is a manufacturer and is manufacturing sufficient pork in this country to feed our people, and is exporting annually millions of dol-Mr. TAYLOR.
lars' worth besides. That is an object lesson of how our farmers can be protected. In the same way we could secure for our farmers the absolute control of our home market for vegetables, which to-day are imported to a large extent from the United States. But my hon. friend is evidently a trimmer. His sole object seems to be to make a speech which will enable him to proclaim himself a free trader in some portions of the country, and then go to the salt manufacturers and others and declare himself in favour of protection.
Let me now address a few words to the government. It is well known that this government came into power in 189(5 over the corpse of the Manitoba school question. The right hon. the Prime Minister promised the people that, if returned to power, the first thing he would do would be to send out a commission, headed by the hon. Sir Oliver Mowat, to Manitoba to investigate the facts of the school question and that he would then settle that question at once and for ever. Did he carry out that solemn promise which he then made to the people ? No, Sir, he did not send Sir Oliver Mowat, but sent another emissary, and managed by some manipulations and manoeuvres, to have the school question smoothed over temporarily and then said :	' Now
the question is settled.' Let me ask whether the people of the, province of Quebec will take the word of the Prime Minister as against that of the high dignitaries of the Roman Catholic Church ? What does the Archbishop of Manitoba say on the question ? He declares positively that it is not settled, and the Archbishop'of Montreal, who has just returned from Rome where he had an interview with) His Holiness the Pope on this very question, also declares that it is not yet settled. Well, for my part, I am prepared to believe the dignitaries of that church rather than the right hon. Prime Minister on this point.
The right hon. gentleman made a promise to the temperance people. He said to them:
' If you elect me to office, I will submit a plebiscite to the people on the question of prohibition.' And I will give effect to the will of the people. He did submit a plebiscite, and then sent down to the province of Quebec three or four of his ministers to tell the people there that if prohibition were carried, it meant an extra two dollars a head of taxation on every man, woman and child in the country, and as every French Canadian family is very large-pretty near 15 being the average French family.
Hear, hear.

speechtext:
present Lieutenant Governor of British Columbia (Sir Henri Joly de Lotbiniere), then Minister of Inland Revenue, and the Minister of Justice (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick) asked the people of Quebec to vote against prohibition on this ground, but notwithstanding all their efforts, the result of the plebiscite was a large majority in favour of putting an end to the liquor traffic. Did my right lion, friend give effect to the will of the people ? Why, that question stands today exactly as it stood before the plebiscite was taken.
Then he promised that if returned to power, he would take the duty off agricultural implements. Did he carry out that promise V He found a tariff of 20 per cent on agricultural implements. That rate still exists on these articles to-day. Did he not also, during the elections of 1890, promise the people free coal oil ? Why, we saw posted on every barn and fence throughout the country the placard :	' Vote for
Laurier and free coal oil.' Has he redeemed that promise ? My hon. friend, who has just spoken, would like to see the government redeem that pledge, but how many years is he going to wait for them to redeem it ? All they did was to reduce the duy one cent a gallon on coal oil, which, I must say, is removing it in a very infinitesimal degree.
The right hon. the Prime Minister likewise promised reduced expenditure. Put me in, lie said, and I will surround myself with a cabinet of business men, and we will fun this country on economical lines. If elected, we will reduce the expenditure $2,000,000 or $3,000,000. The Hon. David Mills said that they would reduce it $5,000,000, but the right hon. gentleman would not go that length. He said he was not prepared to promise a reduction to that extent, but that certainly he would reduce our annual expenditure some $3,000,000 or $2,000,000. Have the government redeemed that pledge? Instead of reducing the expenditure they have increased from $40,000,000 to $03,000.000. They have increased our annual expenditure by about $23,000,000.
The .right hon. gentleman promised to reduce the national debt. Has he done it V Sir, he lias put a mortgage on every farm in this country, which in the aggregate amounted to $13,000,000 taking the whole Dominion, since he came into power. My hon. friend, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (lit. Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright), when in opposition, used to work out how much every extra million dollars of increased national debt amounted to on every farm in the country, and he would exclaim : That is the mortgage put on your farm by this corrupt Tory government. Put us in and we will redeem that mortgage. Have they redeemed it ? On the contrary, although we have the largest revenue this country has ever Jiad, they have run the country into debt, by their extravagant expenditure, on another $13,000,000.
The right hon. gentleman further appealed to the country :	' Put me in and I will
abolish the national policy.' Both the right hon. gentleman and the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce made the same pledge. Put us in, they exclaimed, and there will be no more protection. Have they carried out that promise ? We had the statement of the ex-Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) a few nights ago, that the tariff to-day is practically the same as that which Mr. Foster left. These hon. gentlemen made a few changes, but their tariff is the same old national policy, and the ex-Minister of Public Works stated this much more forcibly than I can do it. Let the members of tiie government settle with their former colleague as to which is right. The people will have no difficulty in deciding between them because there is the tariff. In the one column is set forth the old rate and in another the new rate, and out of a hundred items, not more than probably one or two are changed. Some are changed up and some are changed down.
The next promise made by the right hon. gentleman was that he would reduce the number of cabinet ministers. Has he done that ? Instead of doing that, he took two who were only door keepers in the Conservative government and made them full pledged Cabinet ministers with increased salaries.
And back pay.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
Yes, antedated-away back. Then he promised the people :	We
have one chamber of the Dominion legislature filled with old women. We will abolish that or reform it. Has he redeemed that promise ?
It is reformed.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: It is there just as the Conservative party left it, except that a few of the Conservatives have died.
No, no.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The hon. member for Gaspg (Mr. Lemieux) shakes his head and says it is not quite the same. The only difference is that a few of the Conservative members have died and their places are filled with partisans of the present government.
Old women too.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
Yes, for instance the gentleman who used to represent North Wellington is there. When the Conservative party were in office and that gentleman was in this House, he used to speak of the Senate in no complimentary terms. But he is now a venerable and distinguished member of that body. Then, the Prime Minister promised the people :	Put us in and we
will reduce the taxes on the necessaries of life and put them on the luxuries. I would ask the right hon. gentleman now on what necessary of life have the taxes been re-

cl need, with the single exception of corn, which may be regarded as a necessary of life ? And on what luxuries has he increased the taxes ? On the poor man's luxuries and his alone-tobacco and sugar. Before I sit down I shall give some figures to show the enormous sums that lion, gentlemen opposite have taken out of the pockets of the poor farmers and labouring men of this country by increased taxes on sugar and tobacco last year as compared with the year 1895. Then, while promising the people of the country generally in his speeches that he would abolish the national policy, the premier went to the manufacturers, closeted himself with them, and assured them that they need not he afraid, that his party would not interfere with the national policy. Ask the ex-Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) whether that statement is true or not. He made the statement on the floor of the House, declaring that it was not a cabinet secret, that there was a private, secret bargain made with the manufacturers, that if the Liberals got into power they would not interfere with protection. And so we still have the protection, notwithstanding the promise given to the farmers that it should be abolished and the duties removed. I could go on for a long time setting forth the promises made and broken by the party now in power. But X can quote words more forcible than any I could use, from the utterances of one of their most prominent supporters, a gentleman who has done more, given more time and spent more money in the interests of the Reform party than any of those I see before me. This gentleman wrote a letter, after negotiating with his friends. He thought he had just claim, considering all the time and money he had spent in their interest, to a seat in the Senate. But he found he could not deal with them, as the price was too high. He wrote an open letter, and this is what he said :
It would be utterly wearisome to review in detail all the ugly record of promises made and broken by the present government. I can only glance at some of those not already noted. We declared that the number of paid ministers in the cabinet was too great under the late administration ; we have the same number still and their aggregate salaries are $4,000 per year greater, one-half this sum going into the pocket of the minister who recently declared that every pledge has been kept. We denounced the expenditure on account of superannuation and pledged oursellves to wipe it out ; it was greater by $14,331 in 1899 than it was in 1896. We denounced as useless the creation of the Department of Trade and Commerce. The ' useless ' department has been continued. We promised to abolish the Senate or radically change its constitution ; by affording that body an opportunity to save the country from the consequences of extravagant and corrupt deals, the government has enabled the Senate to demonstrate its usefulness, almost Its indispensability. We denounced the development of monopolies, trusts, and combines as a consequence of the policy of our opponents ; not a single one of those which

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
were in existence in 189S has been destroyed or put out of business

He refers to the coal oil monopoly.
-while others have been created and given a foothold In the country by the direct action of the government. We declared that the expenditure for the administration of justice was too great. Sir Wilfrid Laurier even going so far as to say that thousands of dollars paid to counsel had been improperly If not corruptly paid ; the expenditure of this department has been increased by $353,000. We denounced the expenditure of $120,000 for immigration purposes ; we have more than doubled this expenditure, increasing it to $255,000.
It is $500,000 now.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
Yes, it has doubled up again.
We condemned the granting of public lands as bonuses to railways ; only by the opposition of the Senate was the government prevented from consummating a deal by which twenty-five thousand acres of gold-bearing lands, to be selected by the beneficiaries, was to he given per mile for the building of a narrow-guage tramway, a transaction so flagrantly improper that several government supporters refused to vote for it, and it is doubtful if any one would now he willing to defend it on its merits. We denounced the granting of cash bonuses to railways, declaring it to he 'a fruitful source of jobbery, peculation, and corruption we have well nigh out-Heroded Herod by the reckless way in which we have granted cash bonuses to railways, giving in one Instance for the same railway two millions more than we had condemned our opponents for offering, and in another actually granting a bonus to a road for which no charter had been granted and which was not even projected. We condemned all corruption ; yet our leaders have made us responsible for the Crow's Nest job, by means of which the directors of the leading government organ were permitted to practically grab a quarter of a million of acres of coal lands, and the country is saddled with a totally unnecessary payment of two millions of dollars. Wre promised purity of administration; the history of the notorious Drummond railway job shows what regard our leaders had for such a promise.
But why go farther ?
He stops, as I felt compelled to stop, for it is impossible to cover the whole list.
The record of our party while it has been in power under its present leaders is one long, shameful story of promises unfulfilled and pledges broken ; of reckless extravagance ; of jobbery and corruption ; and of utterly disgraceful betrayal of every principle for which as a party we have stood.
I could not use such strong language if I tried, nor could I draw a more faithful picture of the present government than this that one of their own prominent supporters has drawn up-and he knew the inside work-* mgs of this government.
For the purpose of securing themselves in office the men who have been entrusted with positions of leadership have brought disgrace upon our party and dishonour upon the name of Liberalism. What then is our duty to our party and to our country ? Again I repeat that

only by repudiating these leaders, by disassociating ourselves from them

They are going fast. One honest man has gone out, the ex-Minister of Public Works. He could not swallow it all:
-and by doing all that may be in our power to punish them for their falseness and treachery, by driving them from power and from the offices which they retain as the price of their treason to principle, can we as individuals and as a party avoid sharing their guilt and participating in their shame. In no other way and by no means short of this can we hope to regain or retain as a party the respect and confidence of a patriotic and decency-loving public. It may be said that this can only be accomplished at the expense of a return to power of our political opponents ; a party opposed to the political principles in which we believe. I do not dispute this, nor do I shrink from this alternative. Neither do I believe that any true man or any man who has an abiding faith in the truth of Liberal principles or in the ultimate triumph of truth will shrink from it. We are bound to assume that the Conservative party is permeated and guided by a genuine belief in the truth of its political ideals and in the correctness of its principles. At any rate we cannot truthfully charge that party or its leaders with having betrayed or abandoned its principles to get or retain office.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I could not use stronger language than that used by Mr. H. H. Cook, the writer of that letter.
When did he write it ?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
My hon. friend (Mr. Campbell) knows well when the letter was written, as he knows the contents of it. It was published in all the papers in Canada. But I can find it by looking up the files of the ' Globe ' and ' Mail,' and I will give the date to the hon. gentleman when the House assembles after recess.
At six o'clock, House took recess.
After Recess.
House resumed at eight o'clock.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just before the House rose, at six o'clock, I was reading to the hon. gentlemen opposite the opinion held of them by one of their supporters, a gentleman who supported them strongly in the election of 1896, a gentleman who perhaps gave more time and spent more money in the interests of the Reform party than any other man in Canada. I was reading this gentleman's opinion of hon. gentlemen opposite, and of their conduct since they came into power. The hon. member for West York (Mr. Campbell) asked me when this letter that I read was written. I could not answer him just then, but said that I would do so after six o'clock. I tell him now that that letter was written by Mr. II. H. Cook about the 1st of October, 1900. After the hon. member for West York had asked me that question, the Minister of Customs, whom I am glad to see just now
entering the House, said that we had had an election since then. It is true, we have had an election since then. The hon. gentleman sat in his seat while I was making accusations against the government, and while I read this letter of condemnation, written by Mr. II. H. Cook ; the Minister of Customs, the Prime Minister and the Minister of Trade and Commerce all sat in their seats, and not one of them dared to dispute a word, either of the statements that I made or of the statements made by Mr. Cook. In fact the Minister of Customs practically admitted that the statements were true, because he said: 'We have had an election since then.' As if to say, that wipes out the whole thing. It is true, all that Mr. Cook has said but we have had an election since then, and we are here and you are over there. How will the Minister of Customs make good the statement so far as it applies to the province of Ontario ? Whose word was accepted in the province of Ontario, the word of my hon. friend or the word of Mr. H. H. Cook 1 Why, the Reform party came near being swept out of existence in the province of Ontario, and the Conservative party came hack with a jnajority of over twenty. Where were the Reform party in that province of Ontario where Mr. Cook's letter was circulated, and where the conduct of hon. gentlemen opposite had been ventilated on the platform ? Manitoba, that great province, also sent a majority to support the Conservative party in this House. But we know how the majority supporting the government in this House came to be elected. They did not come from the province of Ontario.
Now, we have here a government conducted by some fifteen ministers, including the Solicitor General. We have a cabinet composed of fourteen members and a Solicitor General, each of them drawing a sessional indemnity of $1,500 a year, and the most of them a salary besides of $7,000 a year. How are these hon. gentlemen earning the salary that this country is paying them ? Have they been sitting here since the Finance Minister made his budget speech ? How many of these ministers that are being paid $7,000 a year by this country and $1,500 a year as sessional indemnity-how many of them are sitting in their seats to answer the charges that may be brought against them ? Why, Sir, the other night the constitution was fairly wrecked when the Finance Minister moved the adjournment of the House, and looking round to find one of his colleagues to second the motion, there was not one of them in his place, and he had to ask a private member to second the motion to adjourn. That is how little these gentlemen think of attending to their duties. Why do we find so many of these ministers scattered to the four corners of the earth, enjoying themselves and having a good time ? Why are

they not sitting here like honest men, earning the salaries paid them by the people of this country as civil servants to administer the affairs of this country ? They go off on jaunts and pleasure excursions at the expense of the country. Look at the Auditor General's Report, and see the vast sums charged for the travel of ministers on their jaunting tours. Where are they to-night ? The Prime Minister, it is true, is not in his place, but he is to be excused, because his health being poor, the members of the House, particularly on this side, would not expect that hon. gentleman to be in his place any evening during the entire session. But where are the other hon. members whom the people are paying $8,500 a year ? They ought to be sitting in their places to answer the charges that are made against them by members on this side of the House in respect of their conduct in administering the affairs of the country. Why are they not here earning their money, the same as members on this side of the House, and those who sit behind the ministers themselves on the other side ?
Let me imagine a large incorporated company, a manufacturing concern that employs a president, a secretary, a treasurer and superintendents of different departments. Similarly we have in this country running the government, in the Prime Minister, a president, we have the Secretary of State, and we have the Finance Minister as treasurer ; then we have superintendents of the different departments. We have the Minister of Trade and Commerce occupying that position which he said there was no use for when he was on this side of the House, and which hon. gentlemen opposite said they would abolish if they ever got into power. But he is sitting there now as a looker-on, drawing his $7,000 a year and his $1,500 indemnity. Why is he not here to-night to answer the questions that I intend bringing up shortly in reference to the trade and navigation returns ? He is not to be found. He is the superintendent of that branch of the business. Then we have the Minister of Inland Revenue, to whose department I intend to refer before sitting down. Where is he 1 Earning his $1,500 indemnity and his $7,000 salary. Is he here to answer to the people of this country for the way he is conducting their affairs ? The Finance Minister is the treasurer ; as is his duty, he has generally been in his place since the debate commenced. But he is practically the only minister out of the fourteen whom we have seen here. My hon. friend sits smiling opposite me, the Minister of Customs, who is the pack-horse of this government, he has been pretty generally in his place also. My hon. friend the Postmaster General is here tonight, but we have not seen much of him since this debate commenced.
I guess they are attending receptions.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The Minister of the Interior, I .have no doubt, is attending a reception across the sea. Well, he should be here attending to the duties of his office, managing the affairs of his department. Why did he find it convenient to clear out just when the session was coming on, going over there to look after the Alaskan boundary ? Could not some other man out of his department have gone over there to do the work that he is doing Is it because he is afraid to face the ex-Minister of Public Works that he is absent There must be some cause for it. Is he afraid to come into the House and face the jobs going on in his department, some of which we have heard of lately from the Yukon. The Minister of Public Works is the other pack horse of the government. He and the Minister of Customs have practically been the representatives of this government during the entire season from the time the House adjourned last spring until within a few days of meeting here, late in March. These two gentlemen are the pack horses of the whole cabinet. They remain here holding the fort, each of them acting for his own department and half a dozen other departments, whose heads were away spending the peoples money and drawing the salaries that I have mentioned. The Minister of Railways and Canals-why is he not in his seat He is paid $1,500 sessional indemnity and $7,000 besides. Why is he not in his seat ?
I guess he is at a reception.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
Oh, yeS, the hon. gentleman and his colleagues are great for receptions. If there is a reception given, either in Japan, or in England, or in any place in Canada, these gentlemen neglect their parliamentary duties and their other duties which they are sacredly charged to perform as the civil servants of the people of Canada. They desert their duties and go away to enjoy themselves and attend receptions. Then there is the Minister of Militia and Defence, we have only seen him in the House a part of two days since this discussion commenced. He should be here to defend his department for conducting which he is paid a heavy salary besides his sessional allowance. Then there is the Minister of Agriculture-where is that hon. gentleman ? Is he another one of those whom the ex-Minister of Public Works referred to as those of his colleagues with whom he was on terms of intimacy ? Is he one of those who are afraid to meet the ex-Minister of Public Works on the floor of parliament ? He is away over in Japan. We saw an account in the papers a day or two ago about his attending a reception over there with the Geisha girls. Is that what the Minister of Agriculture is paid for doing in place of being here attending to his department ? That hon. gentleman is at the head of the most important department of

this whole government, yet we have not seen him in the House during the entire session. How long are the people going to put up with this kind of thing ? Would any business concern allow its president, its secretary, its treasurer and the superintendents of each of the departments to absent themselves from their positions of trust without leave and not bring them to book ? Not an institution in this country would do it. Will the people of this country, once their eyes are opened to the conduct of these hon. gentlemen say to them: You have done well; you have performed your duties faithfully and we will return you to power ? I think nay. They will say that they have been unfaithful stewards and they will make them walk at the next election, come when it may. The hon. Minister of Justice (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick) has been fairly faithful in his attendance in the House but he is not here to-night. We have two hon. ministers out of the fifteen sitting in the House to-night during this debate when every minister ought to be in his place. We have the hon. Solicitor General (Hon. Mr. Carroll). Hon. gentlemen opposite, when they were on this side of the House and when the late Conservative government appointed a Solicitor General, found a great deal of fault with that appointment, but the excuse is made now, that, that having a Solicitor General, a large amount of fees that formerly went to lawyers for transacting the affairs of the country will be saved because the work will be done by the Solicitor General's Department. Look at the Auditor General's Report and you will see that there is not a town or village in this country in regard to which there is not the record of some heeler of a lawyer having been paid large sums of money for attending to the affairs of this country when we have the hon. Minister of Justice and the hon. Solicitor General paid large salaries to look after these matters. We find that the amount paid out in fees for legal services is double and treble that which was paid out under the late government. The hon. Minister of Finance, in introducing his budget, suggested some changes, but very few. I am satisfied that the changes that the hon. minister proposes in the resolutions now before the House are very disappointing to a large class of pfeople in this country, to the manufacturers, the agriculturists and the labouring men. The hon. Minister of Finance, in his budget speech last year, led the people to believe that at this session of parliament there would be a revision of the tariff and that relief would be granted to many important industries in the country. But, the hon. Minister of Finance made no changes on the lines that he had intimated he would adopt at the last session of parliament. Ask the hon. exMinister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) He said and said plainly and above board that there would be changes, that the hon.
Minister of Finance had promised them, he stated so publicly and for having made these statements the hon. ex-Minister of Public Works was walked out of the cabinet. But, the hon. gentleman who succeeded him in the cabinet and who occupies the portfolio of Marine and Fisheries (Hon. Mr. Prtsfon-taine) when appealing to the electors in the election following his admission to the government, made statements stronger than those of the ex-Minister of Public Works; yet, lie supports a government that has repudiated the statements he made when he was seeking the suffrages of the electorate. Tlie hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) moved the following resolution. He said :
I beg to move the following amendment to the motion of the hon. Minister of Finance :
That all the words after ' that ' in the proposed motion be left out, and the following substituted therefor :-' This House regarding the operation of the present tariff as unsatisfactory is of opinion that this country requires a declared policy of such adequate protection to its labour, agricultural products, manufactures and industries as will at all times secure the Canadian market for Canadians ;
' And that the financial policy of the government should include a measure for the thorough and judicious readjustment of the tariff at the present session.'
This is the amendment that is now before the House. The hon. member for West Huron (Mr. Holmes) and others who have spoken have found a good deal of fault with the word ' adequate.' What is the meaning of the word 'adequate.' If I understand tlie English language it means sufficient.
For what ?
speakername: The POSTMASTER GENERAL (Hon. Sir William Mulock).

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Sufficient protection to secure to the manufacturers, to the agriculturists, and to the labourers of this country the work of manufacturing or producing all the articles that we can produce and manufacture in this country by our own labour and keep the money in our own country. Make your tariff sufficiently high to do that.

Would the hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor) allow me to ask him a question. He has defined the meaning of tlie word ' adequate.' Would he tell us what he means ? Does he mean twenty-five per cent, thirty-five per cent, of forty-five per cent ? Specify it.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: No I will not.
He cannot do it.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: My hon. friend was willing to go as high as thirty-five per cent. Now, I am willing to go to the amount sufficient to protect the industries of the country even if it is one hundred per cent.
One hundred per cent.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Yes, one hundred per cent, and there are articles under the tariff to-day that are practically placed at one hundred per cent. The lion. Minister of Customs (Hon. Mr. Paterson) is away above thirty-five per cent on the lines he manufactures. Adequate, in my opinion, means sufficient, and sufficient, in my opinion, and in the opinion of hon. members on this side of the House means that the tariff should be so adjusted as that it will protect our industries without respect to figures. The hon. member for West Huron (Mr. Holmes) will call thirty-five per cent a revenue tariff, or he will call it a free trade tariff, or anything to suit himself, but he will not admit that it is a protective tariff. I want to call the attention of the hon. Minister of Customs to a few figures which I have taken from the Trade and Navigation returns and I think they will be found correct in every particular. I will just name eight different articles that were imported into this country in 1895 and the same articles imported in 1902. In 1895 we imported the following articles

Will the hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor) allow me to ask him, if these were not the very articles that the leader of the opposition is reported to have said were adequately protected now ?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I am not responsible for anything the leader of the opposition said, and further, I don't believe that my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Paterson) heard him say it, and furthermore, I do not believe that the leader of the opposition did say it, because he has explained last year and this year, that adequate protection means sufficient protection to have these goods manufactured in this country.
It is reported that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax) said it, and it has not been denied.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
Oh, there are lots of reports, and I couM give some reports about my hon. friend's (Hon. Mr. Paterson) industry up there, too. The contention of this side of the House, and it is the argument of every man who has the interests of the agricultural and labouring and manufacturing classes at heart; the argument on our side is that every article I have enumerated there should be manufactured in this country so as to give employment to the labour that would consume the produce grown in Canada, and would keep our money at home as national capital instead of sending it to a foreign country.
But let me call the attention of the House to another matter. These gentlemen on the treasury benches promised that when they

got into power they would give free trade and in order to hoodwink the people on the free trade question, they put corn on the free list. What has been the result of that ? In 1896 we imported into Canada 1,485,980 bushels of corn, which paid a duty for all purposes, whether for manufacturing into liquors or otherwise, and we imported free corn to the amount of 262,680 bushels, or a total of 1,748,660 bushels. What was the result last year under the policy of this government ? The duty collected in 1896 was $207,301.29. In 1902 we imported 474,950 bushels of dutiable corn that went into the manufacture of whiskey, I suppose, and paid a duty of $35,609.62, but we imported free corn to the amount of 4,485,372 bushels, a total for the year of 4,959,987 bushels against a total importation in 1896 of 1,748,660 bushels, or a total increase this year in dutiable and free corn over 1896 of 3,211,217 bushels. What does that mean ? It means that these 3,211,217 bushels of foreign corn have displaced the Canadian farmer's products of peas, oats and barley, that would otherwise have gone to feed the pork and the beef that was raised by the Canadian farmer. And in consequence the product of the Canadian farmer had to find a market elsewhere on account of being displaced by American corn. My hon. friend from West Huron (Mr. Holmes) says that the people of his county want free corn. I can tell him that I represent a constituency in which there are as many well-to-do farmers as there are in West Huron, and I do not think that you will find a farmer in my county who will not vote against the importation of free corn. If the farmers of this country would sink their political feeling and speak their minds they would say, that they can grow all the corn and coarse grain needed in this country to supply the market. There is another matter I want to call attention to. The Prime Minister, and the Minister of Customs, and every member of the cabinet, promised that if they got into power they would take the tax off the poor man' and put it on the rich man. They announced that the necessaries of life should be free and that luxuries should be taxed. Let us see what this government did in relation to some of the necessaries of life. Let us see what happened in connection with sugars and syrups. In 1902 we imported of refined sugars above No. 16 Dutch standard, 51,379,428 pounds, on which a duty was collected amounting to $642,278.53; we imported of sugars not above 16 Dutch standard, of all kinds, 318,696,019 pounds, on which a duty was collected amounting to $2,107,149.64. These are the raw sugars brought in to supply the manufacturers of this country, and that is the amount of duty the government collected from that article. Of syrups we imported last year 1,355,552 pounds, on which a duty was collected of $10,104.09. On molasses a duty was collected amounting to $423.84; on sugar candy 634
a duty was collected amounting to $54,248.23; on glucose a duty was collected amounting to $38,177.16, and on sacharine a duty was collected amounting to $64,573.80. On all these articles I have mentioned the duties collected in 1902 amounted to $2,916,955.29, whereas on the same articles in 1895 the duty collected amounted only to $365,796.23, or an increase of duty on the poor man's sugar amounting to $2,551,158.06. Here was over two and a half million dollars wrung out of the pockets of the poor men of Canada, in order to swell the treasury for the government to squander it corruptly. What becomes of their promise that they would take the taxes off the necessaries of life. Sugar is a necessity of life, and yet this government have collected two and a half million dollars on it, more than was collected under the Conservatives in 1895. And the government do this in order to swell their surplus to $13,000,000. Why was it that the Conservative government had not a surplus in 1895 ? It was because the then Conservative government took the taxes off sugar and let the poor people of this country have free sugar. But these hon. gentlemen on the raw materials of the sugar manufacturers of this country collected taxes amounting to over $2,000,000, and the refiners can only take it out of the pockets of the people who consume sugar.
Then the hon. gentleman is not in favour of a duty on sugar ?

speechtext: I am in favour of a duty on manufactured sugar, but not on the raw sugar. I am in favour of admitting the raw sugar free and giving our manufacturers a chance to employ labour in refining it. This is what I am in favour of, and evidently the hon. gentleman is not.
You forget that you put a duty on raw sugar again after you had taken it off.

I have read them ; I have given the quantities and the amounts ; and I think there will be a good deal more of the hon. gentleman's speech not read that will go into ' Hansard ' than of mine. I wish to ask why this government have collected these large amounts of taxes from the poor people of this country on sugar and tobacco and on fruits and vegetables, to put into this overflowing treasury ? It is only for one purpose, that they might, squander this money among their supporters. They have spent the largest amount ever expended in Canada in any one year. Where can they point to any large or important work that they have built during the past year ? It is true, they can point to some wharfs and piers down in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Quebec and to a few in Ontario, and to a few public buildings scattered here and there. Some days ago I asked the question :	what was the
cost of taking the census in 1871, in 1881, in 1891, and the amount paid on account of taking the census of 1901 up to the 1st of March, 1903. The return brought down gave the cost as follows :	In 1871, $511.-
330.40 ; in 1881, $456,904.19 ; in 1891, $570,115.54 ; and in 1901. up to the first of March, 1903, $1,112,900.20. More than double, on the average, what it cost the corrupt Tory government, as my hon. friends opposite used to call them, for taking the census in 1871, 1881 and 1891. And all this increased expenditure was simply to give a place to a lot of party friends

who wanted a job. I do not know that I can do better than read an article published in the ' Weekly Review ' of April 17tli, 1903, which came to my observation a few days ago. The article is as follows :
