speechtext:
The Auditor General's Report under the head ot Dominion census throws some light on the subject ot the expense being doubled, while the publication has been delayed and the returns are less accurate. The process seems to have been to appoint double the number of officials from their party office seekers, and to give each of them the same pay as their predecessors, who did twice as much work.
One expenditure to which the Auditor General objects is that of $1,486, incurred by the census branch investigating the census of 1891. Several men were employed at high salaries to endeavour to ferret out ex parte information that might seem to discredit the former census. For instance, diocesan records were procured, giving lists of the faithful in the various dioceses, and these were shamelessly used in the House as being enumerations of the total population. This expenditure of $1,500 would have an indirect value if Mr. Ross was not a traitor to his province, for he could urge it as a precedent of 1901, which, being fraudulent on the face of it, requires investigating far more than that of 1891.
But the most objectionable expenditure is that for the salary, $2,500, and travelling expenses, $1,032, for Mr. Thomas Cote, assistant special commissioner. This is only from June, 1901 to June, 1902, so it does not include the amount before then, or since, if he is still drawing pay. And we in Ontario have to contribute to this expenditure incurred for the purpose of manipulating the Quebec enumeration so as to defraud us out of our rightful representation in the House of Commons. No excuse can be offered for this appointment. There was no more reason why there should be an assistant special commissioner for Quebec than for Ontario or indeed for any of the other provinces. If the language difficulty were alleged it would be a flagrant false pretense. Mr. Blue, the special census commissioner, already had an assistant commissioner, Mr. E. H. St. Denis, an experienced census official, whose tongue is French though he is equally at home In English. Thus there was already ample provision for the instruction of the Frenchspeaking chief census officers, for correspondence with them, and the county commissioners, and for any other duties requiring a proficiency in French. The only possible reason for the appointment of this unnecessary official is the obvious one of securing an over-enumeration of the population, while no such efforts were made on behalf of Ontario and the other provinces. The object was gained by such an unfair exaggeration of the figures for Quebec as compared -with Ontario that we have been defrauded of six members. To arrive at this conclusion it is not necessary to suppose that Mr. Cotd was dishonest in the execution of his official duties. It would answer the purposes to instruct him and to impress upon his mind the importance of making the best showing possible for Quebec and the propriety of giving the most generous construction to the confessedly doubtful application of the de jure system to non-residents. He would pass this on to the county commissioners and they to their enumerators, who would one and all be ready and willing to carry out such agreeable
instructions. With another instructor for the Ontario chief officers and their subordinates, laying stress upon the necessity of being very careful not to count any persons as to whom there was the least doubt, the relative proportion of the provincial populations could easily be affected. We have no hesitation in charging the ministers who made this improper appointment with having done so with the deliberate intention of robbing us of our rightful representation in the House of Commons.
As we have seen there has been an expenditure of $1,500 to investigate the census of 1891. If Mr. Ross was not so busy with his efforts to cling to his unusurped power instead of looking after the interests of his province, he would demand that a similar amount should be expended in investigating the census of 1901 in this direction. A beginning might he made by examining special schedule A in which the names of non-residents were to be inserted by the enumerators. This might throw some light upon the subject.
Tlmt article, coupled with the return I have just read, shows how this $03,000,000 was expended by this government last year. Everything they touched, every job they did, cost double what it should. Money has been squandered in every direction just as it has been in the taking of the census, on which $1,200,000 lias already been expended, and the work not yet nearly completed. We find that the cost of taking the census in Ontario was double what it was in 1891. That is a fair example of the manner in which everything is conducted. Take up the Auditor General's Report, and you will find that the same vile system was carried on last year, which was in force the previous three or four years-the system of buying goods from party friends and paying two or three times their value. The government buy coal oil at retail price. They pay 32 cents a gallon and $1.25 for the barrel, and last year bought some twenty or thirty barrels. I find that every dollar of public money paid out lias been paid out without competition to political supporters, and two or three times the value of the goods paid. Why does not the government do, as any business man would, have all the buying done, after calling for tenders, and see that the money of the country is fairly and honestly expended ?
Mr. Speaker, I have occupied more time abusing this government than I intended to do and yet I have not said one-half what I could say and which I would be justified in saying.

he said that that great province had returned a majority of twenty Conservatives to this House, and concluded with the very pertinent inquiry :	Where were the Grits
of Ontario ? I can tell the hon. gentleman ; the Grits of Ontario are to-day doing business in those dives where he and his friends bad put them by legislative enactment. But if I cannot agree with my hon. friend on this point, I can agree with him in his heart-felt sorrow that more members of the cabinet are not in their seats when such hon. members as the member for South Leeds (Mr. Taylor) and Haldimand (Mr. Thompson) undertake to address the House. On both occasions, we should have the fourteen cabinet ministers, and the Solicitor General as well, in their places.
Reducing the matter to a cash nexus which the hon. member for South Leeds seems very fond of doing, I have to commiserate him upon the fact that while he made the major part of his speech only Si14,000 worth of ministry, qua ministers, were in their seats-though I am glad to say that to listen to me I have about ?21,000 worth of ministers.

farmers' representative, coming from a county largely agricultural, coming from a county that has no large towns, am free to confess that the farmers of this country have reason to thank the Liberal government for that expenditure upon cold storage. I note the fact that in 1895 the Australians were getting in the markets of England for their butter from two to three cents a pound more than the Canadians were getting. And why ? Because they had good cold storage when we had poor cold storage, or none at all. They brought their butter across the Pacific, then across this great continent, and when they got it into the English market they got that much more from it than we did for our butter, though having to ship it a far less distance. I know that some money was being spent at that time by the Conservative government along these lines. But my charge against them is that when Australia had a system so perfect as that, by which butter could be transported that long distance in perfect condition, it was nothing to the credit of the Conservative government that we could not transport our butter a shorter distance, and that we got the price we did. although we ore now getting a better price for the butter than the Australians. Therefore. I am not going to apologize for that part of the increase of $12,000,000 which lion, gentlemen opposite have dubbed extravagance.
The next item is immigration. Well, I am sure you will admit that not much need be said on the head of immigration. True, we are spending $299,000 more than our opponents spent, but with what result ? We are all rejoiced to see the influx of settlers from the United States and England. Do you suppose they would have come here entirely of their own accord ? No, our immigration agents have been doing excellent work among them, have been sowing the seed, and the harvest time is now upon us, and we are gathering in as a result of their labours.
I think that our friends opposite might better have described the movement under their regime as an emigration movement from Canada, judging from the cancelled homestead entries and other evidences. So I am n it going to apologize for that item.
For quarantine there is an increase of $103,000 over the expenditure by our opponents in 1895. Now, it is necessary to keep disease out of the herds in this country, and when I tell you that a large part of this expenditure has been to indemnify Canadian herdsmen for the slaughter of their diseased cattle and hogs, and in order to preserve Canadian hogs from the hog cholera, you will admit that in the interests of our farming population this was an increase at which nobody can cavil, and I believe lion, gentlemen opposite have made no objection to it. I will not go extensively into the subject of what this government has done in the way of reopening a splendid market in the United States for our live cattle trade. But we do Mr. THOMPSON (HaMimand).
know that in the days of the late government there was such an embargo upon our cattle going into the United States that trade with that country practically failed, and for four years and a half we shipped into that country less than 4,000 head of cattle, and we got back scarcely $50,000. But after the energetic action taken by our new farmer-Minister of Agriculture, through whose agency the restrictions were removed ; this trade went up by leaps and bounds, and one firm, the Ironsides Brothers, among the largest dealers in Canada, is my authority for the statement that the action of the government in getting that embargo removed added $10 a head to the value of the live stock in Canada. When I tell you that we are a beef-eating people in Canada, that we devour something like 100,000 head of cattle per month, the consequence of that statement is readily apparent. If we eat 100,000 head of cattle per month, we devour 1,200,000 head in the course of a year; and at $10 per head that would mean $12,000,000 extra added to the wealth of the farmers of this country by this farmers' government. You cannot get away from the fact, you may say the figures are extravagant, but you wiil admit that there is but one market price for cattle, that if the American buyer comes in and gives a certain price for a two-year-old to take over the line, the local butcher has got to give as much for another two-year-old in the same market. So when you raise the price of our export cattle you raise the price of our cattle for the home market; and we have a right to claim that millions upon millions per annum have been added to the wealth of the farmers of this country by the energetic action of the Minister of Agriculture. Having recaptured this market, is it strange that we should be willing to spend more money to retain it ? We know why the Americans put that embargo on in the first place. They did it because they said that disease existed in our herds. Well, suppose that disease broke out again and became widespread, back goes your embargo, and you would have as hard a time to remove it in the case of the United States, as you are having now in making an unsuccessful attempt to remove it in the case of England. Therefore we cannot consider any expense too great to ward off such a disaster as that coming upon the farmers of Canada. No one will object to the government spending on quarantine fully as much as that service requires.
Now, Sir, I come to militia, and this is a subject in which, as you know, I take considerable interest. But it does not follow that for that reason I should burden you long with a discussion of that part of our increased expenditure. Suppose we say the increase is $486,694. Analysing it, there is an increase in pay and in wages, and the increased pay to the permanent officers and men and to the militia civil servants

amounts to $76,000. Well, Sir, we know that wages have increased all along the line, in every walk of life; and instead of accusing this government of extravagance in the matter of the militia, I would rather charge them with jjarsimony of the most , extreme kind, in that year after year they take our young fellows to the front and pay them fifty cents a day, when at home they might make $1.50. I ask hon. gentlemen to note how independent I am, how I criticise the government when there is occasion for it; therefore when I support the government hon. gentlemen should give more weight to my remarks when they see how fair-minded I am. Next we come to military property. There is an increase of $141,000. We found the military properties which we took over from hon. gentlemen opposite were all tumbling down. I know whereof I speak, I am not taking the blue-books for my authority. I have been an enthusiastic militiaman for nearly twenty years, I have kept in touch with this subject, and I pledge my personal knowledge that these buildings were in a wretched condition. Indeed they are in none too good a condition now, but they are infinitely better than they were when hon. gentlemen opposite had them in charge. So once more I will not apologize for that increase, but I rather blame the government for not having made it a little larger. In military stores the same remark applies. There is an extra expenditure of $48,000. I think it well to have good rifles in this country, we have very few of them, but they are quite useless without cartridges to place in the chambers of those rifles. Especially would you find yourself in an awkward position if you were standing at 2,000 yards opposite another fellow who had ammunition and you had none.
Then we come to the matter of clothing, where there is an increase of $110,000. And that leads me to say that in the old days of the Conservative regime only half the militia was drilled every year. That was a most disastrous thing. The fellows went down for twelve days at a time, and as two years had to elapse before they were turned out again, they forgot practically in the meantime all that they had learned in those twelve days. Wiser counsels have prevailed with this government in this matter, with the result that we now drill them yearly. Now, would you expect us to go to drill every year and wear out as little clothing as we would if we drilled only once in two years ? We have spent $110,000 more in clothing; in addition to that our stores are in better shape so far as supplies and clothing go than they have been in many a long year past.
Then we come to the Dominion cartridge factory. Gentlemen, I would not have you think for a moment that I am one of those loud mouthed jingoes who wish to see a large standing army in Canada, who would
like to see this country' borne down by military expenditure. I believe my views are pretty much the views of hon. gentlemen on both sides of this House as I have heard them expressed many and many a time. I agree that we should as far as possible encourage the practice of rifle shooting in this country, but you cannot have rifle shooting without cartridges. The cartridge factory at Quebec has been enlarged and increased in order to deal with the new situation created by the civilian rifle clubs which are in existence and which hon. gentlemen opposite never inaugurated and as a consequence of that the factory has been improved to such an extent that now it will be able to turn out three times as many cartridges as in times gone by. If you take these items you will find that they more than account for the total increase of $468,000. Then, we come to the mounted police. The increase is $302,090, but as more than that amount of money was actually spent on the force in the Yukon, and the Yukon as we all know, taking it from the first until the present, has practically paid for the Yukon, there is no increased burden on the people. With an expenditure of a little more than $8,000,000 and with receipts of a little more than $8,000,000, the receipts are less than the expenditure by about $200,000, covering a term of years. So, I make the broad statement that the Yukon lias paid foi the Yukon and having paid for the Yukon it has paid for the mounted police in the Yukon. This apparent increase of $302,000 is not really an increase because the money has come back. Next we come to public works and here is the largest individual Increase we have except in the case of the collection of revenue of railways and canals. We find that the increase in this department came to $2,478,970 but wliat more do we find ? The only way to proceed in analysing matters of this knd is to compare them with the doings and the expenditures of hon. gentlemen opposite when they were in the government. I have heard the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) time and again say :	We
refuse to be bound by those old comparisons. Let the dead past bury its dead. But if we do not make this comparison what are we to do ? We cannot compare anything with the Conservative party's present because it is not charged with the expenditure of money, we cannot compare it with its future because we are not sure it will have any future. So, we are bound to compare it with its past. If we proceed on this principle we find simply this : that the hon. ex-Minister of Finance (Mr. Foster) in 1896, in liis main and supplementary estimates, and I will admit that he did not bring down the supplementary estimates but they were drafted by the government, they, were found and read-in his supplementary estimates he was willing to spend the sum of $3,998,-

610 for public works. We have spent on public works $4,221,293, or we have spent more than he was willing to spend only about $225,000. But, mark you, in that year he had a revenue under $34,000,000 with a deficit of $4,000,000 and in this year we had a revenue of $58,000,000 with a surplus of $7,000,000-a very different case indeed. But, I need not have gone so explicitly into this argument because I think this is one of the increases that no one can object to. Liberals cannot attack it because this expenditure has been made by a government in which they have every confidence and hon. gentlemen opposite should not attack it because this is the expenditure of a man to whose virtues for many years they were blind, hut their eyes have been opened and they have discovered that that hon. gentleman was the brains of the Liberal cabinet. Will these hon. gentlemen cavil at the expenditure of the hon. ex-Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) ?	1 take it that they will not.
Therefore, I pass to the next item. It is mail subsidies and steamship subventions $111,688 of which I need say little. We have been opening up new trade channels, and establishing new lines between Canada and South Africa, and the requirements of the country are such that the increase is justified. The next we come to is ocean and river service in which there was $291,997 of an increase. This is almost wholly accounted for by the purchase of two new steamers and the balance by the increased cost of wages and supplies which we meet all along the line and which we all know in every walk of life has advanced considerably since 1895. Coming to fisheries, we have an increase of $105,000. I do not find that any of our friends from the maritime provinces objected to that. I imagine that cold storage for the preservation of bait has something to do with this increase but when we take into consideration the benefit it has been to the fishermen of the maritime provinces I am sure hon. gentlemen will admit that there is ample justification for it. Then, coming to subsidies to provinces, we find an increase of $151,423. This is a matter that is statutory. We know very well that as population increases, these provinces getting so much per head, their subsidies must increase and that accounts for the whole amount save except a small item we saw fit to pay the province of Prince Edward Island and which one of the hon. members on the other side, at present in his seat, will, I think, not dispute, was a just and honourable payment to that province. And so, we come down to Indians. The increase in the vote for Indians is $101,726. There was a time when we sang with the poet ' lo, the poor Indian.' But we do not look very much to the poor Indian just now for the good reason that he has lost his franchise. I ask hon. members of this House as practical politicians and as great statesmen if they will not agree with me when I say that in Mr. THOMPSON (Haldimand).
the disbursements for Indians, politicians are not under the temptation to give the Indian more than his due. The increase in the expenditure from the government of the North-west Territories is very easily dealt' with. There is an increase of $188,297. It is an increase certainly, but they are our wards and as the country fills up we have more services to perform until the time comes when they set up housekeeping for themselves and then this expense will be replaced by a subsidy. my department, they put it under the miscellaneous head with the result that there is great comfort for the souls of some of the cabinet ministers. I think hon. gentlemen will agree with me when I say that not only was that criticism in had taste but it showed a lack of the knowledge of business principles as well. After the Prince and Princess had been sumptuously entertained in New Zealand, Australia and even in South Africa, I think it would have been unfitting if Canada had brought up in the procession at the tail end without a few brass bands and a little bit in the way of fireworks. If you were to come down to the cash basis to the mere question of advertising, and recollect that the heir apparent to the Crown was accompanied on that tour by some of the brightest newspaper correspondents in England, that they were cabling reports every day to the old land, that these reports were being copied throughout the British Isles in the provincial press- if we are to come down to the patent medicine argument, to the question of advertising, considering, the advertisement which Canada got, the money was well spent. Well, we got something in return for that; we get fire protection and free water, and I am told that is worth $15,000 or $20,000 a year. Shall we follow the example of other great nations; although we may not in strict accuracy be a great nation yet; we are on the way to it and as sure as the sun rises and sets so sure we will he a great nation.
Hear, hear.
Hear, hear. .

I consider myself as good a Britain as any . of you, but I am that and more too-I am a good Canadian. And when the British government, or some of the British statesmen had made up their minds that Canada would collect money to hand over to them for expenditure, then I say that it is a good thing for Canada, aye and for Britain, too, that they should not be kept in the dark, that that matter should be at once set at rest, and that they should know over there that we in Canada enjoy a self-government, one tittle or particle of which we do not propose should be taken from us; and, that any money we collect for imperial objects or otherwise will be spent through our own channels.
Hear, hear.

Then we come to the purchase of the Plains of Abraham. I think that lion, gentlemen opposite will agree with me that that is perhaps the most interesting landmark in the country. We knew that the Plains of Abraham were about to be broken up into building lots, and this government came to the rescue and paid $80,000 for that historical landmark. And we know, Sir, that that was done by our generous French Canadian premier, supported by the French Canadian members of this House, who are broad enough and good enough Canadians to feel that in that battle on the Plains of Abraham, there was no disgrace for either race, and that the column erected to the joint memory of Wolfe and Montcalm in the city of Quebec, typifies the feeling of union that now exists in the descendants of those men who locked arms on these very Plains of Abraham.
Some hon. MEMJmRS. Hear, hear.
Then we pass on to the grant given to Marconi, amounting to $70,000.
Eighty thousand dollars.

$80,000 in all, but $70,000 expended in 1902. Why, it only shows the enterprise of the government ; that is all. Marconi's scheme was poo-poohed; capitalists interested in cable companies and all that gave him the cold shoulder; he was thwarted in every way. plied money in aid of genius. More than that, this government did not do it for nothing. The idea of thrift came into the transaction; there is a streak of canniness in it; the Scotch members of the cabinet look after that. They said : Yes, Mr. Marconi, we are willing to help you, and if this thing comes to be successful we would like a little help in return. And so the cabinet arranged that if the matter does come out all right they are to get the services of Marconi's various offices at a greatly reduced rate; at a rate so much reduced that in a few short years the amount of the expenditure will be recouped to the government and we will be money ahead. Then we come to the banking service in the Yukon which cost $53,169. That is merely money spent in connection with the collection of the dues on gold mining in the Yukon. It all came back from other sources and it cost the people of Canada nothing. Then we spent $50,000 to aid the unfortunate sufferers in the West Indies. I believe that the hon. gentlemen opposite raised not one dissenting voice as to that item. I do not think there is a man in the House who would raise a dissenting voice against it. I believe we are all united in doing something for these unfortunates so heavily visited by the hand of Cod. and although they were our brother colonists I believe Canadian generosity would go even further than that, and that in the case of any great national calamity, whether the sufferers were brethren within the empire of some time enemies without the empire, we would be willing and glad to give them our assistance in some small degree to alleviate their sufferings. Next I come to an item so small that you will almost wonder why I am quoting it. It is the expenses of the half-breed claims commission, amounting to $10,161. The half-breeds in the North-west had some grievances, had presented these grievances to the government, and what did the government do ? It sent out a commission and the cost of that commission is a little over $10,000. It is the association of ideas and not the amount that leads me to mention the sum. In the early eighties the half-breeds of the North-west had some grievances also, and they petitioned the government again and again but the pigeon-holes yawned for these petitions. Petition after petition was forwarded to the government only to meet with the same fate, and as a result we had a c'rl 1"wRebellion, which cost the people of Canada $5,000,000 and scores of valuable

Hear, hear.

And now in that large increase of $928 000 for miscellaneous expenditure I have given Mr. THOMPSON (Haldimand).
you items which total $S27,000, and the remaining $100,000 is composed of items so minute that it would take at least an hour to go into them, and I cannot weary the House that long, but if you refer to the books you will find that there is as good justification for every cent of the increase as there is justification for the items I liav.e given to you. The expenditure on the Yukon provisional district was paid for by the Yukon, and it did not cost the people of Canada one cent. And yet the ' Mail and Empire ' published an editorial in connection with a late interesting election contest in a constituency called North Ontario, in which it stated that the Yukon is running us behind, that there was a large deficit and that the hon. member for West York (Mr. Campbell) was trying to qualify for cabinet rank because he was trying to out-well, I won't use the word, because it would be unparliamentary-but at all events, to outstate the other cabinet ministers who had been in the riding, when he said that the Yukon had paid for the Yukon. That editorial in the ' Mail ' contains a half truth, and nothing more or less. It is true that during this last year there will be a deficit if we include public works in the Yukon, but if you take the expenditure and receipts 'from the beginning of the world unto the day of the date of these presents' the Yukon has paid for the Yukon. That is what has occurred in the Yukon. Now, there is an increase in the customs of $258,391. Well, is that probably rather a questionable increase ? As a matter of fact, having known the Minister of Customs since I was a very small boy, I have had a good deal of confidence in him throughout all that time, and frankly I must say that I never knew him as an extravagant man in any sense of the word whatever. He has carried his methods of economy into his department, and I have heard many business men who are not Liberals in politics, say that a better Minister of Customs Canada never had. When you consider the immense increase in revenue which the hon. minister is called on to collect, you will readily see that he cannot hope to bear the expense of his department with the same amount with which it was borne in 1895. But this he can say and prove, that so far as percentages go, he has collected every $100 of duty at far and away less cost that our Conservative friends did in 1895, even if he shows a total increase in the cost of that department of $258,000.
Nextwe come to the Post Office Department, in which the increased expenditure is $429,989, and I touch on this subject with some diffidence, because it is a subject on which I feel that I am sitting at the feet of Gamaliel. Yet in talking about the Post Office Department I feel that I am on safe ground, and I propose to take up the cudgels for a few moments. And here I wish to pay a compliment to the hon member for Botli-well (Mr. Clancy), who, I am sorry to see

is not in his place to-night-a fact to which I call the attention of the hon. member for South Leeds (Mr: Taylor) because in the event of a change of government, the hon. gentleman would be slated for a cabinet position, and if he does not stay in the House lie is not training very well for the place in which he expects to earn a salary of $7,000. besides getting $1,500 indemnity. I have always entertained a feeling of respect for the hon. member for Botliwell, and to this feeling I must now add a degree of admiration for his courage in attacking tlie administration of the Tost Ofliee Department ; because in the splendid galaxy of ably administered departments which we have in this government, there is no bright particular star more bright than that department. It is a subject on which we all like to talk when we are discussing administrative economy, and I will take up the statement of the hon. member for Bothwell and examine it. One grievance of the hon. gentleman is that the jubilee stamps which were issued by the hon. Postmaster General and were bought largely by the people of Canada, cannot now be redeemed in the currency of the realm. I wonder if the hon. gentleman is largely loaded up with this non-negotiable security. The hon. gentleman said that the Postmaster General took advantage of a loyal wave that was sweeping over the country to sell those stamps at the time ; and, I suppose to complete the argument, now that the loyal wave has subsided, he will not buy his stamps back again. I think the hon. member for Bothwell must have invested a large sum of money in those stamps when liis loyalty was at the boiling xioint, and now that it is simmering down, he has a grievance against the lion. Postmaster General because he will not relieve him of his investment. But what is astonishing to me is that the hon. gentleman, belonging as he does to the party of loyalty, cannot find some one in the party whose loyalty has not cooled, and who will relieve him of his purchase made at an unwary moment. The consequence is, the hon. gentleman says, the minister got half a million dollars by the trick, and that is the way he reduced the deficit. True, he did, and I think he was fire tty clever in doing so. But he did it in one year only ; he did not repeat the offence. What lias that to do with the receipts and expenditures for this year ? Nothing whatever, and yet he has an absolute surplus this year, when you make a fair comparison, of over $5,000. The hon. gentleman says that the hon. Postmaster General eliminates the Yukon and the Atlin districts, and were they not parts of Canada ? What a splendid headline it would make for some of the Dawson papers, that the Postmaster General is insinuating that these districts are not parts of Canada ! But this is poor argument for the hon. member for Bothwell. Of course, they are a part of Canada, but they were not until this government discovered that they were ; that is the point. The Conservatives were not spending money on the Yukon and Atiln districts in 1895, and when the hon. Postmaster General wishes to make a comparison between his administration and that of his predecessors, why should he not eliminate what cost them nothing ? When he does that, he has a surplus for this year of $5,000. But there is a discrepancy between the report of the hon. Postmaster General and the Public Accounts, and the ' Mail and Empire,' with briny tears in its eyes, asks who cooked the accounts ; and it makes me a very flattering offer which I cannot refuse to accept. Referring to a speech I made in North Grey, it says :
Sir William Mulock publicly announced that he had scored a profit ot $5,000 ; but the post office report reports a. loss of $82,375, while public accounts show a loss of $105,221.'
And here. Mr. Speaker, is where I have hopes of future greatness :
If Colonel Thompson can explain away these unfortunate discrepancies he is an excellent calculator.
Think, Mr. Speaker, what it would mean for me if I could go back to my constituency with the ipse dixit of the ' Mail and Empire' that I was an excellent calculator. It is worth making the attempt, and that attempt I wish to make now. There is that discrepancy between the report of the hon. Postmaster General and the Public Accounts, but that discrepancy will be found to exist where a similar discrepancy was the year before ; and if you take the receipts and expenditures of the two years and work them out together, you will find that they work out dollar for dollar. The hon. Postmaster General did actually expend $105,000 in excess of his receipts, including the Yukon and Atlin districts in this particular year ; but part of that was for expenditures incurred during the previous year ; and therefore, adding the two years together, you will find that while his statement makes him about $28,000 better this year than do the Public Accounts, his statement of last year makes him that much worse off than they make him. It is simply a matter of bookkeeping. The hon. Postmaster General's administration of his department is such as would be a credit to any man, and hon. gentlemen opposite in cavilling at it, only expose themselves to ridicule.
Coming to the Public Works Department, the increased cost in the collection of revenue was $340,815. But the Atlin and Yukon telegraph lines and the telegraph lines in connection with the gulf service account for almost the whole of this amount, especially if you add $48,000 which was expended for the cable vessel the ' Tyrian.'
Then we come to the largest individual increase, the Railways and Canals, in which

tlie increase cost of collection of revenue was $2,801,350 ; but tlie increase of revenue amounts to $2,751,531 ; so that if bon. gentlemen will note the two amounts they will find that the money comes rolling back into our coffers within $50,000 of the whole amount. Therefore the people of Canada must not be led to believe that we are spending money to that extent. We are operating more railways and canals, that are not supposed to pay directly, and next year the discrepancy may be still greater, because the government have announced their intention of making the canals as free as the ocean itself. This will, of course, involve an increased cost to the country, but the results in the form of a reduction of freight rates will redound to the advantage of the shippers and farmers of the country. Hon. gentlemen opposite may say that you are taxing the people more, because in this particular you are taking more out of their pockets than you are giving back. But the reverse is more likely to be the case, and the argument is as fair one way as the other.
The cost of the administration of justice in the Yukon last year increased $115,526, but it has come back to us in the form of Yukon royalties. It is not fitting that I should pass this matter over without saying a word on the administration of justice in the Yukon. I believe that our administration of justice in that distant country is one of the proudest incidents in the national life of Canada. We all know the enormous difficulties which must be met in maintaining law and order in such a distant and sparsely settled country, and we all know that law and order is maintained there as well as it is this night in the city of Ottawa. We know that no murderer can go unpunished there, that though it may cost $100,000 to hunt him down-and I believe in one case it did cost more than that-Canadian justice has an arm long enough and strong enough in the Yukon Territory to seize him and make him pay the penalty. So far from our increased expenditure on this head being a disgrace to us, we can take credit for it.
Now, I have accounted-and I believe fairly and reasonably accounted-for more than $12,125,000 of increase. What remains over is little indeed. I could even account for that but to do so would compel me to go into items of very small expenditure with which I must not weary the House. But the general argument applies, even if I refrain from the particular, with regard to these few items, and the general argument is that with an increase of trade in the country such as we are now enjoying, you cannot expect to carry on public business with the same amount of money as before. This reminds me of an epigramatie saying of the great Napoleon, which is particularly applicable to the point I am making. When, after a famous battle his soldiers reported Mr. THOMPSON (Haldimand).
very heavy losses in killed and wounded, his invariable reply was, with a shrug of his shoulders ' on ne fait pas d'omelette sans easser des oeufs.'
Five minutes more, Mr. Speaker, and I think I can finish. The increase in our public debt, if we can take the estimate of the Minister of Finance for the expenditures of the current year-and we are now so used to find his estimates correct that we can have no hesitation in accepting them- the increase in our national debt will be $7,681,657 at the close of the current year, or a little more than $1,000,000 per year since this government has taken office. Can we not account for some of this increase ? If we take the South African war and the Halifax garrison, which was of course part of the expenditure on the South African war-that garrison having been made a Canadian garrison to relieve the British soldiers-we find that the expenditure on that head amounted to $2,830,965. That is an expenditure which certainly nobody can complain of, but it forms a considerable portion of the increase in the public debt. Then there is the discount on the Fielding loan of 1897, amounting to $826,317. But we can offset against that discount the benefit which my hon. friend the Finance Minister obtained for Canada by succeeding, for the first time in its history, in floating a loan at an interest of two and a half per cent, and thus establishing a rate for investors in tlie case of future loans. This loan is generally conceded by financiers to have been an extremely good piece of finance. But inasmuch as we have to charge that loan against our capital debt at par and did not obtain par for it, we have to take that discount of $826,317 as one of the items which account for the increase in the public debt. But it is an item against which no possible objection can be raised, because we get the benefit of a lower rate of interest, which in a number of years, will more than offset the discount. It is an expenditure in one sense, but it is an expenditure which comes back to our pocket in much the same way as does the sinking fund. Then there is the cost of the expenditure caused by the eastern extension railway award, namely, $671,836 in Nova Scotia and $280,692 in New Brunswick. This expenditure was the result of an arbitration arising out of the complications incurred by the late government and wiped out by this government. It represents therefore an increase in our debt for which the present administration cannot be held responsible. Then take the purchase of the Drummond County railway, which cost $1,464,000. But we have the railway and we have by this means brought the Intercolonial railroad into Montreal. That certainly is an expenditure for which we have abundant justification and in return for wliich we. have good value to show. The next item to which I will call the attention of the

House is the arrears of the Post Office Department amounting to $685,000. When my hon. friend the Postmaster General took charge of that department, he found that not only were there yearly deficits but a large amount of old debts actually remaining unpaid, and which were carried over from year to year. Being desirous to make expenditure and revenue balance each year, so that we could tell exactly where we stood, my hon. friend asked parliament for a special vote of $685,000 to pay the debts incurred by hon. gentlemen opposite. Had hon. gentlemen opposite paid off these debts, the expenditure in their time would have been increased to that extent and also the public debt, and therefore we are not fairly chargeable with that amount of increase. I find next an item of $745,964 paid for arms contracted for by the late government, and for which they left us to pay the piper. This too should not be charged against the present administration. Then there is the sum of $500,000 paid in the settlement of claims in Manitoba, which were left unsettled by the old government. This certainly can not be charged against the present administration. Adding all these items together, they aggre-. gate over $8,000,000 and hundreds of thousands more might be added in the same way of moneys expended because of circumstances extraordinary and unique in their nature or because of the necessity to pay debts incurred by Conservative governments. So that if we eliminate expenditure caused by the South African war and the debts which hon. gentlemen opposite should have paid but did not, you will find that we have not added one dollar to the public debt of the country, and more than that we have poured out millions like water in developing our canals and railways and making proper provision for the public works and general service of the country.
I must apologize, Mr. Speaker, for having detained this House so long listening to figures at this stage of the debate, when everybody is tired. I have no more comments to make on the budget beyond congratulating my hon. friend the Minister of Finance on the excellent showing he was able to make to the people of Canada and on the increasing prosperity which the country is enjoying under the able administration of this government.

X desire, Mr. Speaker, to make a few remarks on the very important subject we are now discussing, but at this late hour, I do not wish to detain the House, and I would therefore beg to move that the debate be adjourned.
The evening is still quite early and if my hon. friend desires an adjournment I do not wish to press him to go on.
